pages.title: Nutrition plan
pages.tagline: Energy, protein and four meals fitted to a 12:00-04:00 day, calibrated against your own scale.
pages.summary: Your nutrition plan has fixed points and one moving part. The fixed points: about 140-155 g of protein a day (1.8-2.0 g per kg of body weight), at least about 60 g of fat, at least 30 g of fibre, and four meals timed around your 12:00 wake, 13:00 training, 16:00-01:00 shift and 04:00 bedtime, each with at least about 31 g of protein. The moving part is energy. Equations put your maintenance near 2,700 kcal a day, but their individual error is several hundred kcal, so the calibration period (Phase 0 plus Phase 1 weeks 1-2) replaces the guess with your own number from two to three weeks of weighed food logging and daily weigh-ins. Phase 1 then runs at maintenance to 300 kcal below it, a range in which untrained men can often lose fat while still gaining muscle; a small surplus or a moderate deficit can follow, depending on what your check-ins show. Carbohydrate fills the remaining energy and is concentrated before and after training. Much of what people worry about, such as meal frequency, a narrow post-workout window or eating after midnight, matters little once these targets are met.

sections.title: Targets at a glance
sections.body:
These are starting values for you at 31 years, 181 cm and 77 kg, with an estimated body fat of about 20% (plausibly 17-24%) and a [[term:ffm|fat-free mass (FFM)]] of about 61.6 kg (58.5-63.9 kg). Energy is set relative to your *calibrated* maintenance, the intake at which your weight holds steady (your [[term:tdee|total daily energy expenditure (TDEE)]]); the kcal figures below use the provisional 2,700 kcal/day until your calibration (Phase 0 plus Phase 1 weeks 1-2) replaces it. [[term:recomposition|Body recomposition]] means losing fat while gaining muscle at roughly stable weight.

| Goal | Energy vs maintenance | At the provisional 2,700 kcal | Weight trend to aim for | When |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Calibrate | Eat normally, log everything | Measured, not set | None: the trend is the data | [[phase:p0]] |
| Recomposition | 0 to -300 kcal/day | 2,400-2,700 kcal | 0 to -0.25 kg/week | [[phase:p1]] default, see [[dec:D04]] |
| Lean gain | +150 to +300 kcal/day | 2,850-3,000 kcal | +0.1 to +0.25 kg/week | When recomposition stalls and you are leaner |
| Dedicated fat loss | -300 to -500 kcal/day | 2,200-2,400 kcal | -0.5 to -0.7% of body weight a week (0.4-0.55 kg); never faster than 1% | Optional block of 8-16 weeks |

| Nutrient | Rule | For you, per day | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Protein | About 1.8-2.0 g/kg (range 1.6-2.2) | 140-155 g | Floor 125 g (1.6 g/kg) as a 7-day average; 2.0-2.4 g/kg (155-185 g) in a fat-loss block |
| Fat | Default about 1.0 g/kg (25-30% of energy); floor 0.8 g/kg | About 75 g; at least 60 g | Never below 20% of energy |
| Carbohydrate | The remainder | About 300-350 g in recomposition; roughly 370-440 g in a lean gain | 40-50% of it in meals 1 and 2 |
| Fibre | At least 30 g, or about 14 g per 1,000 kcal | 35-40 g | Raise over 2-3 weeks if you eat less now |
| Water | Drink to thirst; pale-straw urine | About 2.5-3.5 L in hot months (inference) | More on hot training days |

**Why these numbers**

- **Energy.** Equations put your [[term:ree|resting energy expenditure (REE)]] at roughly 1,630-1,950 kcal/day: Mifflin-St Jeor gives 1,751 [@Mifflin1990_REE], and fat-free-mass-based equations give about 1,630-1,940 depending on the equation and your uncertain FFM [@Cunningham1991_FFMequation; @tenHaaf2014_athleteREE]. Multiplying by a [[term:pal|physical activity level (PAL)]] of 1.4-1.6 gives about 2,450-2,800 kcal, and the US National Academies equations for inactive to low-active men give 2,680-2,900; hence 2,700 as the provisional figure. The standard error of a predicted energy expenditure is about 340 kcal/day for men [@NASEM2023_EER], larger than the recomposition and lean-gain adjustments in the table, which is why you calibrate.
- **Recomposition first.** Simultaneous fat loss and muscle gain is well documented in untrained and overweight people, and also occurs in trained lifters [@Barakat2020_recomp]. Resistance training alone lowers body fat by about 1.5 percentage points on average [@Wewege2022_RTbodyFat], and lean-mass gains shrink as the deficit grows, disappearing on average at about 500 kcal/day [@Murphy2022_deficitLeanMass]. Your [[term:whtr|waist-to-height ratio]] (0.45-0.48) is already below the 0.5 boundary [@Browning2010_WHtRboundary], so there is no health urgency for fast fat loss (inference).
- **Protein.** Extra protein during training increases fat-free mass [@Morton2018_proteinRT; @Nunes2022_proteinLBM], with the benefit flattening at about 1.6 g/kg/day in a between-trial analysis [@Morton2018_proteinRT] and smaller but non-zero gains above about 1.3 g/kg in another [@Tagawa2021_doseLBM]. Setting 1.8-2.0 g/kg covers the uncertainty in that breakpoint, food-logging error and the lower digestibility of dal-based protein (inference). In a deficit, protein above the RDA reduced lean-mass loss (by about 0.4 kg on average in pooled trials) [@Hudson2020_aboveRDA; @Helms2014_deficit].
- **Fat.** Low-fat diets lowered total testosterone modestly ([[term:smd|standardised mean difference (SMD)]] -0.38, [[term:confidence-interval|95% CI]] -0.75 to -0.01) [@Whittaker2021_lowfatT]. No source defines a minimum, so the 0.8 g/kg floor is a conservative judgement.
- **Fibre.** Fibre intakes of 25-29 g/day and above were associated with 15-30% lower all-cause and cardiovascular mortality than the lowest intakes [@Reynolds2019_carbQuality]. The 14 g per 1,000 kcal figure is a common guideline convention (practical convention).

Background: [[sci:sci-energy]], [[sci:sci-protein]] and the protein decision [[dec:D19]].

sections.title: Calibrating maintenance (Phase 0 and Phase 1 weeks 1-2)
sections.body:
The goal is one number: the daily intake, in your own logging units, at which your weight holds steady. Two weeks of careful data replace a formula that can be several hundred kcal off.

**Protocol: 14 days (extend to 21 if the trend is unclear)**

1. Weigh yourself every morning after waking and using the toilet, before food or water, in the same clothing. Enter it in [[tool:checkin]].
2. Eat roughly to the targets above, but weigh and log everything: raw ingredients where possible, cooking oil and ghee weighed on the scale, milk and sugar in chai, snacks at work.
3. Keep everything else steady: the same training plan, the same creatine dose (starting or stopping creatine shifts body water and the scale; inference) and no deliberate diet.
4. On day 14, let [[tool:energy]] fit the weight trend across all 14 days, or compare the average of days 8-14 with days 1-7.

**Reading the result**

- Flat trend (within about 0.1 kg/week either way): your mean logged intake is your maintenance.
- Rising or falling trend: correct by about 110 kcal/day for each 0.1 kg/week. Maintenance ≈ mean logged intake + (kg lost per week × 1,100), or minus if you gained. Example: you logged an average of 2,450 kcal and the trend is -0.2 kg/week, so maintenance ≈ 2,450 + 220 = 2,670 kcal/day.

The 1,100 factor is the 7,700 kcal-per-kg approximation divided by 7 days. It is reasonable for the first few weeks of a change (inference) but overestimates weight change over months, because expenditure falls as weight falls [@Thomas2013_3500kcalRule; @Hall2011_energyImbalance]. That is why calibration windows are short and repeated.

**Why logging error matters less than you might fear**

Self-reported intake is biased: in a doubly-labelled-water study, people with obesity who believed they were ‘diet-resistant’ under-reported intake by 47% and over-reported activity by 51%, while their expenditure was normal [@Lichtman1992_underreporting]. Weighing food shrinks the error but does not remove it. Calibration sidesteps the problem: if you consistently under-log by, say, 10%, your measured ‘maintenance’ also reads 10% low, and every later target expressed in the same logging units still lands where intended (inference). The method breaks only if your logging habits change, so keep the same scale, app and routine.

**Expected noise**

- Any change in carbohydrate or salt moves glycogen and water: each gram of glycogen is stored with about 3-4 g of water [@Kreitzman1992_glycogenWater]. Ignore day-to-day swings of 0.5-1 kg.
- In one small study, weight tended to peak after weekends and fall through the week [@Orsama2014_weightRhythms]; compare whole weeks, not single days.
- Equations err in both directions for Indian men: weight-adjusted resting expenditure was lower in Asian-Indian than in Chinese men [@Song2016_AsianIndianREE], yet all eight equations tested underestimated measured resting expenditure in 30 professional Indian weightlifters, by 375-636 kcal/day [@Joseph2017_IndianWeightlifterREE]. Your scale settles it.

+> If illness, travel or a festival week falls inside the window, extend it to 21 days rather than guessing.

Re-calibrate every 4-6 weeks and after every 2-3 kg change in weight, using the routine under Adjusting over time.

sections.title: Your eating day
sections.body:
Four meals at the same clock times on training and rest days, each with at least about 0.4 g/kg of protein (31 g or more). The anchors are the 13:00 session, the 16:00 start of work, a break around 19:30-20:00 and the 04:00 bedtime.

| Time | Meal | Protein | Carbohydrate, fat, fibre | Example (approximate values) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12:00 | Wake; 400-500 mL water | | | Caffeine, if used, goes with meal 1 ([[plan:supplements]]) |
| 12:15 | **Meal 1**: moderate, easy to digest, about 45 min before training | 30-40 g | 40-70 g carbohydrate; at most about 15 g fat and 5 g fibre | 300 mL toned milk, 1 scoop whey, 1 banana, 30 g oats |
| 13:00-14:05 | Training | | Water | 0.75-1 L bottle in hot months |
| 14:45 | **Meal 2**: the largest meal | 40-45 g | 80-120 g carbohydrate; normal fat and fibre | Curry of 100 g raw chicken breast, 30 g raw dal, 2 rotis, 50 g raw rice, 200 g vegetables, 100 g curd; take creatine, D3 and B12 here |
| 19:30-20:00 | **Meal 3**: packed, at the work break | 30-40 g | Normal mixed meal | Soya-chunk curry (30 g dry chunks), 30 g raw dal, 2 rotis, salad, 100 g curd |
| 01:30-02:00 | **Meal 4**: after work, protein-rich, finished by about 02:00 | 35-45 g | Moderate size, not a feast | 3-egg bhurji, 150 g hung curd, 1 roti, 200 g vegetables |
| 04:00 | Sleep | | Fluids tapered from about 02:30 | |

With 200 g of fruit somewhere in the day and 20-25 g of cooking oil in total, the examples come to about 155 g protein, 2,550-2,650 kcal, 70 g fat, 330 g carbohydrate and 40 g fibre: inside the recomposition band at the provisional maintenance. To move energy up or down, change rice, roti, oats and oil; keep the protein foods fixed.

Swaps (approximate values):

- Meal 1 without whey: 2 whole eggs and 3 egg whites, 2 slices of bread, 1 banana, 200 mL double-toned milk (about 35 g protein, 60 g carbohydrate).
- Lighter meal 1: 200 g curd, 25 g whey, 1 banana, 40 g poha or oats (about 30 g protein, 60 g carbohydrate).
- Vegetarian meal 4: 100 g paneer, 200 g curd, 200 mL milk, 1 roti (about 35 g protein; higher in fat).
- Oily fish such as sardine or mackerel (150 g raw) can replace chicken in meal 2 on two days a week, which also covers omega-3; rohu and other freshwater fish do not.

**Why this shape**

- *Meal 1 before training.* You wake after a fast of about 10 hours and train an hour later. Fasted and fed resistance training did not differ significantly in fat-free mass, muscle size or strength in a [[term:meta-analysis|meta-analysis]] of 4 trials, with very low certainty and wide intervals [@Vieira2025_fastedRT]; acute carbohydrate improves resistance-training performance mainly when the comparison is a fasted state [@Henselmans2022_carbRT], which is your situation; and the size and timing of the pre-exercise meal determine how urgent post-exercise protein is [@Kerksick2017_ISSNtiming]. A small, low-fat, low-fibre meal 45-60 min out is the usual compromise for stomach comfort (practical convention). If eating that soon after waking causes nausea or reflux, train with water only and eat meal 2 within an hour of finishing; prefer the fed option on interval days.
- *Meal 2 as the largest.* It refills glycogen and supplies protein after training, and it is your last unhurried meal before work. There is no hard per-meal ceiling after whole-body training: 40 g of whey raised [[term:mps|muscle protein synthesis (MPS)]] about 20% more than 20 g [@Macnaughton2016_20v40], and 100 g of protein produced a larger and longer (over 12 h) anabolic response than 25 g [@Trommelen2023_100g], so a 45 g meal is not wasted.
- *Four feeds of at least 0.4 g/kg.* About 0.4 g/kg per meal over at least four meals reaches 1.6 g/kg/day, and up to 0.55 g/kg per meal reaches 2.2 [@SchoenfeldAragon2018_perMeal]; 20-40 g every 3-4 hours is the consensus pattern [@Jager2017_ISSNprotein].
- *Meal 4 as your pre-sleep protein.* Nightly pre-sleep protein (27.5 g) increased strength (summed [[term:1rm|one-repetition maximum (1RM)]] +164 vs +130 kg) and quadriceps growth over 12 weeks compared with a non-caloric placebo, but total daily protein also differed, so timing and amount are confounded [@Snijders2015_presleep]. 20-40 g of casein about 30 min before sleep raises overnight protein synthesis [@Reis2020_presleepProteinSR]; curd, hung curd, paneer and milk are casein-rich, which is why they appear here. Eating within 1-3 hours of bedtime was associated with more night waking in observational studies [@Chung2020_mealProximitySleep; @Iao2021_bedtimeEatingATUS], hence finishing about 2 hours before 04:00. Add a small casein-rich snack around 03:30 (300 mL milk or 150 g hung curd) only if meal 4 ended before about 01:30 or the day is short of protein.

> Your clock is shifted, not your physiology: on your schedule 01:30 is roughly what 21:30 is for someone who sleeps at midnight (inference). See [[plan:sleep]] for light and caffeine timing and [[dec:D20]] for the full reasoning.

On rest days keep the same four times; meal 1 can be larger and slower to digest, and your supplements move to the first meal.

sections.title: Protein foods that fit your budget
sections.body:
Values are approximate: check labels or the Indian Food Composition Tables (IFCT 2017) for what you actually buy. ‘Raw’ and ‘dry’ mean weighed before cooking, which is how to log them.

| Food | Realistic serving | Protein | Energy | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chicken breast, boneless | 100 g raw | 22-23 g | 110-120 kcal | Lean; curry-cut with bone gives less meat per 100 g |
| Eggs, whole | 3 large | 18-19 g | 210-220 kcal | About 5 g fat each; cheap per gram of protein |
| Egg whites | 3 | 10-11 g | About 50 kcal | Protein without fat |
| Fish (rohu, sardine, mackerel) | 150 g raw | 25-30 g | 150-300 kcal | Oily fish twice a week also covers omega-3 |
| Paneer, full-fat | 100 g | About 18 g | 260-300 kcal | About 20-25 g fat, so count it |
| Curd (dahi), toned milk | 200 g | 6-7 g | About 120 kcal | Casein-rich; good in meal 4 |
| Hung curd (strained) | 150 g | 11-15 g | 140-160 kcal | Straining roughly doubles protein per gram |
| Milk, toned | 300 mL | 9-10 g | About 175 kcal | Double-toned for fewer kcal |
| Dal (toor, moong, masoor) | 30 g dry (one katori cooked) | About 7 g | About 105 kcal | Also fibre; lower digestibility (below) |
| Chickpeas (kabuli or kala chana) | 50 g dry | 9-10 g | About 180 kcal | Soak and pressure-cook |
| Soya chunks | 30 g dry | 15-16 g | About 105 kcal | Usually the cheapest concentrated protein |
| Tofu, firm | 100 g | 10-15 g | 100-150 kcal | Brands vary widely: read the label |
| Whey (sports concentrate or isolate) | 1 scoop, 30-33 g | 22-25 g | 120-130 kcal | Optional; Indian quality issues in [[plan:supplements]] |
| Roti; rice | 1 whole-wheat roti; 50 g raw rice | 3-4 g; about 3.5 g | 100-120 kcal; about 175 kcal | Cereals add up: 5 rotis give about 15-20 g |

**Quality, not just quantity.** In Indian adults, true ileal digestibility of the indispensable amino acids was 89% for whole boiled egg and 92% for cooked chicken [@Kashyap2018_eggMeatTID], against 75% for chickpea, 72% for yellow pea and 63% for hulled mung bean, which dehulling raised to 71% [@Kashyap2019_legumeTID]. Protein-quality scores such as [[term:diaas|DIAAS]] are built on this kind of digestibility measurement. With adequate total protein, soy and animal proteins gave similar gains in muscle and strength [@Messina2018_soy]. Practical consequences (inference):

- Aim for about 60% of daily protein (85-100 g) from eggs, chicken, fish, dairy, soya chunks or whey, and about 40% from dals, legumes and cereals.
- Prefer dehulled dals and soaked, pressure-cooked whole legumes, and pair a cereal with a legume in the same meal.
- When a meal's protein comes mainly from dal, chana or rajma, add about 20-25% (40 g on paper instead of 32 g) or add curd, egg or paneer.

**Budget.** At approximate 2024-25 urban prices, the protein foods for a 150 g day cost roughly INR 3,500-4,500 a month, plus INR 2,000-3,000 for a daily scoop of whey (inference). Soya chunks and dal are usually the cheapest grams of protein and whey among the dearest. Note your local prices and compare cost per 10 g of protein before buying powder.

+> If milk disagrees with you, curd, hung curd and paneer are usually better tolerated, and whey isolate better than concentrate (practical convention).

sections.title: Carbohydrate, fat and fibre
sections.body:
Once energy and protein are right, the split between carbohydrate and fat is mostly a matter of preference, training performance and food quality.

**What matters**

- *Carbohydrate around training.* In the fed state, carbohydrate is unlikely to limit sessions of about 10 or fewer [[term:hard-sets|hard sets]] per muscle: 15 of 17 longer-term diet-and-training studies found no effect of carbohydrate intake, and acute benefits appeared mainly against fasted controls [@Henselmans2022_carbRT]. So put 40-50% of daily carbohydrate into meals 1 and 2 (practical convention). No carbohydrate is needed during sessions of 75 min or less; if 4 × 4 intervals after lifting start to fade, try 20-30 g during the session, such as a banana or 300-400 mL of a 6-8% carbohydrate drink (inference). Going below about 2.5 g/kg (190 g/day) while training most days is not planned in any phase (judgement).
- *A fat floor.* At least 20% of energy and 0.8 g/kg (about 60 g/day), because of the testosterone signal above [@Whittaker2021_lowfatT]. Weigh cooking oil (20-25 g/day in total is a workable budget; mustard, groundnut or rice-bran) and keep ghee or butter to about 10 g/day (the saturated-fat limit is inference, not reviewed here). Include 15-25 g of nuts or seeds daily.
- *Fibre, vegetables and fruit.* Aim for 35-40 g of fibre. Highest versus lowest fibre intakes were associated with lower incidence of coronary heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer, and in trials higher fibre lowered body weight, systolic blood pressure and total cholesterol [@Reynolds2019_carbQuality]. Each extra 200 g/day of fruit and vegetables was associated with about 10% lower all-cause mortality, with risk still falling up to about 800 g/day [@Aune2017_fruitveg]. Target at least 400 g of vegetables (including about 100 g of leafy greens) plus 200-300 g of whole fruit; make at least half your cereals whole grains or millets (whole-wheat atta, parboiled or brown rice, jowar, bajra, ragi, oats); eat pulses daily. Raise fibre over 2-3 weeks to spare your gut.
- *Ultra-processed food.* In an inpatient crossover trial with diets matched for presented energy, sugar, fat, fibre and sodium, people ate about 500 kcal/day more on the ultra-processed diet and gained weight, while losing weight on the unprocessed one [@Hall2019_UPF]. Limit packaged snacks and namkeen, biscuits, instant noodles, sugary drinks, packaged sweets and processed meats to about one serving a day, and 3-4 a week in a fat-loss block (thresholds are judgement). Protein powder is an accepted exception.

**What matters little at equal energy and protein**

- *Low-carbohydrate versus low-fat.* In controlled feeding, lower-fat diets produced trivially more fat loss (about 16 g/day) [@HallGuo2017_dietComposition]; over 12 months, healthy low-fat and healthy low-carbohydrate diets gave similar weight loss (-5.3 vs -6.0 kg), and no genotype or insulin marker predicted who did better [@Gardner2018_DIETFITS].
- *Glycaemic index.* It showed weaker relationships with health outcomes than fibre and whole grains [@Reynolds2019_carbQuality]; you need not track it.
- *Time-of-day carbohydrate rules.* No reviewed source supports avoiding rice or carbohydrate after a certain hour on your schedule (inference).

!> The exception is a ketogenic diet. Combined with resistance training, it reduced fat-free mass by about 1.3 kg relative to non-ketogenic diets [@AshtaryLarky2022_ketoRT]; avoid it while muscle gain is a priority.

The Dietary Guidelines for Indians 2024 organise eating around 10 food groups [@ManojShah2025_DGIcomparison]. Use them as your meal-planning frame (cereals and millets, pulses, eggs and flesh foods, milk products, vegetables, fruit, nuts and seeds, fats and oils), but remember they are general-population guidance: their protein figure (an adult allowance of about 0.83 g/kg/day; background value, not verified here) is an adequacy level, not a training target.

sections.title: How to track
sections.body:
**Kit.** A digital kitchen scale with 1 g resolution and a tare button, a food-logging app with an Indian food database and barcode scanning, and a bathroom scale kept in one place. Workouts stay in Hevy ([[plan:logging]]); weight and waist go into [[tool:checkin]] (measurement details in [[plan:monitoring]]).

**Logging rules that keep error small (practical convention)**

1. Weigh solids raw and dry where you can: rice, dal, atta, oats, chicken, soya chunks. Database entries for ‘cooked dal’ or ‘chicken curry’ vary enormously.
2. For home-cooked curries, build a recipe once: weigh every raw ingredient into the pot, including oil; weigh the cooked contents; then log your portion as a fraction of the total weight.
3. Weigh oil and ghee. A tablespoon of oil is about 14 g and 120 kcal, and unmeasured oil is probably the largest hidden error in home cooking (inference).
4. Log milk and sugar in chai, biscuits at work and tastes while cooking.
5. Check that each meal reaches about 31 g of protein.
6. Prefer label values over generic entries, and check whether an entry is per 100 g raw or cooked.

**How long to log in full**

- Calibration (Phase 0 plus Phase 1 weeks 1-2): every item, every day, for 14-21 days.
- Then keep full logging until the weight trend has behaved as predicted for about 4 weeks (practical convention).
- After that, loosen: log protein only, or 2-3 representative days a week, while daily weighing and the weekly waist measurement continue. Return to full logging for 1-2 weeks whenever the trend drifts outside its band at two reviews, at every phase change and at the start of a fat-loss block.

!> Precise tracking suits some people and wears others down. If logging starts to feel compulsive or food choices become anxious, drop to protein-only tracking and the scale trend, and read [[sci:sci-behaviour]]. Physique-focused sport carries a raised risk of eating and body-image disorders [@Helms2014_contestPrep].

sections.title: Adjusting over time
sections.body:
Targets are hypotheses; your weight trend, waist and lifts are the test. Every 3-4 weeks run the check-in in [[tool:checkin]]; [[tool:energy]] does the arithmetic, and [[rule:energy-adjustment]] and [[rule:phase-nutrition]] hold the decision rules.

**The core rule.** If the smoothed weight trend sits outside your phase's target band by more than about 0.1 kg/week at two consecutive reviews, change intake by 100-200 kcal/day, mostly from carbohydrate and fat. Keep protein fixed. Never react to a single weigh-in.

| Phase | Target trend | Trend below the band | Trend above the band | Other signals |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Recomposition | 0 to -0.25 kg/week | Add 100-200 kcal | Remove 100-200 kcal | Waist stable or falling while lifts rise means it is working, even at flat weight |
| Lean gain | +0.1 to +0.25 kg/week | Add 100-150 kcal | Remove 100-150 kcal | Navel waist rising more than 1 cm a month: cut the surplus by 100-150 kcal (judgement) |
| Fat loss | -0.5 to -0.7% of weight a week; never over 1% | Add 100-200 kcal | Remove 100-200 kcal | Estimated 1RM falling on 2 or more main lifts for 3 weeks: slow the loss and raise protein towards 2.4 g/kg |

**Why targets drift.** Maintenance falls by roughly 24 kcal/day for each kg lost, and rises similarly with gain, because a smaller body costs less to run [@Hall2011_energyImbalance]. Sustained deficits also trigger [[term:adaptive-thermogenesis|adaptive thermogenesis]]: in a modern re-run of the Minnesota semi-starvation experiment (32 lean young men eating 50% below maintenance for 3 weeks), a far larger deficit than yours, resting expenditure fell 266 kcal/day, about 108 kcal/day more than tissue loss explained [@Muller2015_MinnesotaRevisited; @Rosenbaum2010_adaptiveThermogenesis]. Expect fat loss to slow over weeks; that is physiology, not failure. Recompute protein whenever your 7-day average weight moves by 2 kg or more.

**Fat-loss rate.** In one small trial in elite athletes, losing about 0.7% of body weight a week increased lean mass, whereas faster loss did not [@Garthe2011_weightLossRate]; in adults with overweight or obesity, at equal total weight loss, gradual loss removed about 1 kg more fat and better preserved resting expenditure [@AshtaryLarky2020_rateMA]. In a 4-week trial in young men, eating 2.4 g/kg of protein allowed lean gain even in a 40% deficit with hard training [@Longland2016_highProteinDeficit]. Cap a fat-loss block at 8-16 weeks (judgement). One-week ‘diet breaks’ at maintenance every 3-6 weeks are optional: in resistance-trained adults they did not change fat or fat-free mass but reduced hunger [@Peos2021_ICECAP].

**Lean-gain rate.** In trained lifters a 15% surplus added more skinfold fat than maintenance without measurably thicker muscles, although bench press strength rose more [@Helms2023_surplus]; no surplus size has been validated for hypertrophy [@Slater2019_surplus]. During overfeeding, two-thirds of the rise in expenditure came from [[term:neat|non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT)]] [@Levine1999_NEAT], so part of any surplus is burned off. The small surplus suits ‘athletic, not bulky’.

!!> **Guardrail.** Keep [[term:energy-availability|energy availability]] (intake minus exercise energy, per kg of fat-free mass) at or above 30 kcal/kg FFM a day: with FFM of about 61 kg, intake minus exercise energy of at least about 1,830 kcal/day, and never below 25 kcal/kg. Low energy availability causes [[term:reds|relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs)]] in men as well as women [@Mountjoy2023_REDs]; in a narrative review of case studies of male physique athletes, prolonged availability below about 25 kcal/kg FFM was linked to muscle loss and hormonal and mood disturbance [@Fagerberg2018_LEAmale]. See [[rule:energy-availability]].

**Sleep in a deficit.** In 10 overweight adults, cutting time in bed from 8.5 to 5.5 hours during 14 days of caloric restriction reduced fat loss from 1.4 to 0.6 kg and increased fat-free mass loss from 1.5 to 2.4 kg [@Nedeltcheva2010_sleepCaloricRestriction]. If sleep falls below about 6.5 hours on several nights in a week, shrink or pause the deficit until it recovers (pragmatic trigger; see [[plan:sleep]]).

sections.title: Hydration and heat
sections.body:
None of the reviewed sources covers hydration in heat, so this section is standard fluid-replacement practice and inference rather than cited evidence.

- **Daily.** Drink to thirst and aim for pale-straw urine. In hot months total fluid is typically about 2.5-3.5 L/day at your size; a high-protein diet adds a little to the water needed to excrete urea (inference).
- **On waking.** 400-500 mL of water with meal 1.
- **13:00 sessions.** In heat, or in a gym without effective air-conditioning, carry 0.75-1 L and sip about 150-250 mL every 15-20 min.
- **Learn your sweat rate.** Weigh yourself before and after 3-4 hot sessions (same clothes, after using the toilet) and keep losses below 2% of body mass, under about 1.5 kg. For each kg lost, drink about 1.25-1.5 L over the next 2-4 hours, with salted food (meal 2) or an oral rehydration solution if you lost more than 1 kg or trained for more than 60 min in heat.
- **At work.** Keep a 1 L bottle at the desk and refill it once or twice during the shift.
- **Before bed.** Taper fluids from about 02:30 so you are not woken to urinate.
- **Sports drinks** are unnecessary for sessions of about an hour; they add sugar and energy.

!!> Stop training, cool down and get help if you become confused, feel faint, start vomiting or have a throbbing headache with nausea during or after exercise in heat. Heat illness can be an emergency; see [[plan:safety]].

sections.title: What not to worry about
sections.body:
- **Meal frequency.** With energy and protein equal, eating more often does not change body composition; an early signal in its favour came from a single study [@Schoenfeld2015_mealFreq]. Four meals suit your day; three is fine on a busy day if the totals are met (then about 45-55 g of protein per meal).
- **A narrow ‘anabolic window’.** After adjusting for other factors, protein timing had no effect on hypertrophy or strength, and total daily protein was the strongest predictor [@Schoenfeld2013_timing]. Post-exercise protein does raise MPS, and the larger and more recent the pre-training meal, the less urgent it is [@Kerksick2017_ISSNtiming]. Eating meal 2 within 1-1.5 hours is convenient, not critical.
- **A 20-30 g per-meal ‘cap’.** The often-quoted 20 g plateau comes from acute studies measuring synthesis for 4 hours after exercise, both after lower-body (leg) exercise [@Moore2009_doseMPS; @Witard2014_wheyDose]. After whole-body training 40 g beat 20 g [@Macnaughton2016_20v40], and 100 g produced a larger, longer response than 25 g [@Trommelen2023_100g].
- **Time-restricted eating.** In resistance-trained people it did not change fat-free mass and produced small fat-mass reductions (-1.25 kg), most plausibly by lowering intake [@Ali2026_TRE_RT]. Your four meals already span about 12:15-02:00; compressing them adds nothing you need.
- **Eating after midnight.** On your clock, 01:30 is the evening meal of a day that ends at 04:00. What matters is the gap before sleep (about 2 hours, as above), not the wall-clock time (inference).
- **High protein and your kidneys.** In healthy adults, higher-protein diets did not change kidney function over the trial durations studied [@Devries2018_kidney]. If you have known kidney disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, kidney stones or a single kidney, get medical advice before going above about 1.2-1.6 g/kg/day (inference). Creatine and meat eaten the day before both raise serum creatinine without kidney harm; see [[plan:supplements]].
- **Plant versus animal protein.** At adequate totals, soy and animal protein produced similar gains [@Messina2018_soy]; just allow for lower legume digestibility as described above.
- **Fasted training.** Acceptable on days you cannot face food; muscle and strength outcomes did not differ significantly from fed training, with very low certainty [@Vieira2025_fastedRT].

pages.title: Supplement review
pages.tagline: What to keep, drop or avoid, with doses and timings fitted to your 12:00-04:00 day.
pages.summary: Of the nine items you take, three are worth keeping for anyone in your position: creatine monohydrate at 5 g a day, the only one with clear effects on long-term muscle and strength gains, plus vitamin D3 at 1,000 IU and a modest vitamin B12 dose, which are cheap insurance against deficiencies that are common in India. Caffeine reliably improves performance, but on your schedule its cost is sleep: take 150-200 mg with meal 1 at about 12:15 on training days, at most one more 100 mg finished by 17:00-18:00, and none after 19:00. Magnesium glycinate, omega-3 and L-theanine are optional, because none has a demonstrated training benefit in healthy, well-fed young men; keep each only for a stated reason. Stop vitamin K2 and folic acid unless a doctor prescribed them: K2 has no indication at 31, and unneeded folic acid can hide B12 deficiency. Whey is simply food, worth buying only if it is the cheapest way to fill a protein gap, and worth choosing carefully, since independent Indian testing found many mislabelled or contaminated products. Do not add HMB, beta-alanine, nitrate, citrulline, pre-workouts, fat burners or ashwagandha.

sections.title: Verdicts at a glance
sections.body:
These verdicts assume you are healthy, take no regular medicines and eat animal foods every day. A doctor's prescription for a documented deficiency overrides anything here. Your exact products and doses were not available for this review, so check each label against the doses below. Evidence certainty uses four labels: *established* (consistent evidence with intervals excluding no effect, or an authoritative reference value), *probable* (direction likely, size or applicability uncertain), *uncertain* (low-quality, imprecise or conflicting evidence) and *inference* (reasoned from mechanism or arithmetic, not tested directly). *Background* marks a figure taken from standard references rather than from the sources reviewed for this programme.

| Item | Verdict | Dose | Timing | Why | Evidence certainty |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Creatine monohydrate | **Keep** | 5 g/day, every day | Meal 2 (about 14:45); meal 1 on rest days | About 1.1 kg more lean mass and moderately larger strength gains than training alone [@Desai2024_creatineBodyComp; @Wang2026_creatineThreeLevelMA] | Established |
| Vitamin D3 | **Keep** | 1,000 IU (25 µg)/day | Meal 2, which contains fat | About two-thirds of Indian adults are deficient [@Siddiqee2021_SouthAsiaVitDPrevalence], and you spend most daylight hours indoors (inference) | Established (deficiency risk); uncertain (performance) |
| Vitamin B12 | **Keep** | 250-500 µg/day, or 1,000 µg three times a week | Meal 2 | Deficiency in about half of people tested in India [@Venkatesh2021_IndiaMicronutrientDeficiency]; cheap; no established upper limit (background) | Probable |
| Caffeine | **Optional** | 150-200 mg (2.0-2.6 mg/kg) before training; at most one more 100 mg; under 400 mg/day | 12:00-12:15 with meal 1; any second dose finished by 17:00-18:00; none after 19:00 | Reliable acute performance gain; late doses cost sleep [@Guest2021_ISSNcaffeine; @Gardiner2023_caffeineSleepMA] | Established at 3-6 mg/kg, probable at your 2-2.6 mg/kg (performance); probable (sleep cost) |
| L-theanine | Optional | 100-200 mg | With the 12:00 caffeine only | Small acute attention effects, probably driven mostly by the caffeine; no training effect shown [@Payne2025_theanineMA; @Camfield2014_theanineCaffeineMA] | Uncertain |
| Magnesium glycinate | Optional, as a 4-week trial | 100-200 mg elemental magnesium | Meal 4 (01:30-02:00) | Sleep data are low certainty and come from older adults with insomnia; no cramp benefit [@Mah2021_magnesiumInsomniaMA; @Garrison2020_magnesiumCrampsCochrane] | Uncertain |
| Omega-3 (fish oil) | Optional | 250-500 mg EPA+DHA/day, only if you eat oily fish less than twice a week; never over 1 g/day | Meal 2 | No added muscle mass; strength effect fragile [@Uchida2024_omega3RT_MA; @Heileson2023_fishOilRTyoungRCT] | Probable (no effect on mass) |
| Vitamin K2 | **Remove** | - | - | Insufficiency clusters in children and adults over 40, and trial evidence rests on surrogate markers in other groups [@Theuwissen2014_vitKStatusHealthy] | Uncertain |
| Folic acid | **Remove** | - | - | No indication, and unneeded folic acid can hide B12 deficiency | Established (upper limit and masking) |
| Whey protein | Optional, as food | 1 scoop (22-25 g protein) on days whole food falls short | Meal 1, or wherever protein is short | Extra protein helps only up to your daily target; Indian product quality varies [@Morton2018_proteinRT; @Philips2025_CitizensProteinProject2] | Probable |
| Ashwagandha | **Do not add**; avoid it in blends too | - | - | Uncertain benefit; idiosyncratic liver injury, including deaths in India [@Philips2023_ashwagandhaHILI_India] | Established (harm occurs; incidence unknown) |
| HMB | **Do not add** | - | - | No effect on fat-free mass, fat or strength in young adults [@Jakubowski2020_HMByoungMA] | Probable |
| Beta-alanine, nitrate, citrulline, BCAAs | **Do not add** | - | - | Suited to 0.5-10 min efforts or endurance, or already covered by your protein | Background; inference |
| Melatonin | **Do not add** routinely | - | - | Your schedule is stable; darkness, light and caffeine timing come first | Background |
| Pre-workouts, fat burners, ‘testosterone boosters’ | **Do not add** | - | - | Undisclosed doses and herbal extracts | Inference |

**Your daily schedule**

| Time | Training day | Rest day |
|---|---|---|
| 12:00-12:15, meal 1 | Caffeine 150-200 mg; L-theanine 100-200 mg if kept | Caffeine up to about 100 mg if wanted; creatine, D3, B12 and omega-3 (if kept) with this meal |
| 13:00-14:05 | Training | - |
| About 14:45, meal 2 | Creatine 5 g, D3 1,000 IU, B12, omega-3 if kept | - |
| 16:00-18:00 | Optional single coffee of up to 100 mg, finished by 17:00-18:00 | Any caffeine finished by 15:00 |
| 19:00-04:00 | No caffeine, including chai at the work break | Same |
| 01:30-02:00, meal 4 | Magnesium 100-200 mg elemental, during a trial only | Same |
| 04:00 | Sleep ([[plan:sleep]]) | Same |

**Upper limits used on this page** (regulatory reference values for adults; background, not among the reviewed sources)

| Nutrient | Upper limit | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Vitamin D | 4,000 IU (100 µg)/day | IOM; EFSA kept the same value in 2023 |
| Magnesium from supplements | 350 mg elemental/day | IOM; set on diarrhoea; magnesium in food does not count |
| Folic acid (synthetic) | 1,000 µg/day | IOM; folate in food does not count |
| Caffeine | 400 mg/day; 200 mg per single dose | EFSA 2015; healthy, non-pregnant adults |
| EPA+DHA from supplements | 1 g/day | A ceiling chosen for this programme (judgement), because of the atrial-fibrillation signal described under omega-3 |
| Vitamin B12 | None established | No adverse effects known at oral supplement doses |

**If money is tight** (supplements paid from your INR 20,000 monthly food budget): first enough food protein and energy ([[plan:nutrition]]), then creatine (about 150 g a month), then vitamin D3 and B12, then coffee as you like it. Drop K2 and folic acid now; drop L-theanine and magnesium unless a trial shows a benefit you value; drop omega-3 capsules once you eat oily fish twice a week. Supplement prices were not researched for this programme.

Background: [[sci:sci-supplements]] and the decision record [[dec:D21]].

sections.title: Creatine monohydrate: keep
sections.body:
**Verdict.** Keep 5 g of plain creatine monohydrate every day, about 150 g a month. It is the only item in your stack with established effects on long-term gains in muscle and strength.

**Mechanism.** Creatine and phosphocreatine buffer ATP through the creatine kinase reaction (PCr + MgADP + H⁺ ⇌ Cr + MgATP), which sits near equilibrium and regenerates ATP during maximal efforts whose ATP turnover far exceeds oxidative supply. This is the [[term:phosphocreatine|phosphocreatine system]]; phosphocreatine can fall by more than half within 10-30 s of maximal work (background physiology). Muscle takes up creatine against a steep gradient through the Na⁺/Cl⁻-coupled transporter SLC6A8, up to a ceiling of roughly 150-160 mmol/kg dry muscle, beyond which extra intake is excreted. Your own synthesis (renal AGAT, then hepatic GAMT using S-adenosylmethionine) and the meat and fish you eat supply creatine, but supplementation is what pushes stores towards that ceiling (background physiology). Supplementation raises intramuscular creatine and improves high-intensity performance and training adaptations [@Kreider2017_ISSNcreatine]; the plausible route to extra growth is slightly more work per set, repeated over many weeks (mechanistic reasoning).

**Evidence.** In a [[term:meta-analysis|meta-analysis]] of [[term:rct|randomised controlled trials]] in adults under 50, creatine plus resistance training increased lean body mass by 1.14 kg more than training with placebo ([[term:confidence-interval|95% confidence interval (CI)]] 0.69 to 1.59), and lowered body-fat percentage by 0.88 points (-1.66 to -0.11) and fat mass by 0.73 kg (-1.34 to -0.11); training status, carbohydrate co-ingestion and training volume did not change the effect [@Desai2024_creatineBodyComp]. A three-level meta-analysis of 63 studies (1,489 participants) found moderately larger strength gains (Hedges g, a [[term:smd|standardised mean difference (SMD)]], 0.54 for the upper body and 0.55 for the lower body) and smaller effects on lean mass (g 0.30) and body-fat percentage (g -0.14) [@Wang2026_creatineThreeLevelMA]. Part of the lean-mass gain is water: creatine is osmotically active and enters muscle with Na⁺ and Cl⁻, and both [[term:dxa|DXA]] and [[term:bia|bioelectrical impedance (BIA)]] count the extra intracellular water as lean tissue (mechanism). Direct measures of muscle size show a smaller, less certain effect: muscle thickness 1.0-1.6 mm greater than with placebo (pooled effect 0.11, 95% credible interval -0.02 to 0.25), possibly more in younger adults [@Burke2023_creatineRegionalHypertrophy]. Expect the strength effect to be the one you notice.

**Dose and timing**

- 5 g a day; a narrative review of physique-athlete nutrition likewise suggests 3-5 g [@Iraki2019_offseason]. No loading phase is needed: whether trials used loading, and the daily dose, did not change outcomes [@Wang2026_creatineThreeLevelMA]. Loading (about 20 g a day for 5-7 days) only saturates muscle sooner, in about a week rather than about a month (background), at the price of a faster jump on the scale and more stomach upset (inference).
- Take it with meal 2 on training days and meal 1 on rest days. Once muscle is saturated, the daily dose only tops up a pool that degrades to creatinine at about 1.7% a day (background), so clock time matters little and consistency matters most (inference).
- Stir it into water, milk or curd; sediment in cold water is harmless. Keep it out of your pre-training coffee: one early loading-phase trial reported that high daily caffeine blunted creatine's effect, later work mostly did not confirm it (background, not among the reviewed sources), and taking them hours apart costs nothing (inference).
- If it upsets your stomach, split it into 2 × 2.5 g with two meals (practical convention).
- Plain monohydrate is enough. Hydrochloride, ‘buffered’ and ester forms cost more, and no reviewed source shows an advantage.

**Scale and body-composition readings.** Expect body weight to rise by roughly 0.5-1.5 kg as muscle saturates, mostly as intracellular water (background figure from loading studies). Keep the dose unchanged through the calibration period and every later phase, including any fat-loss block, so that this water does not distort your weight trend or BIA readings ([[plan:monitoring]], [[dec:D23]]). If you have not taken creatine daily for the past 4 weeks, start now and read the first month's rise as water, not fat (inference).

**Safety**

- *Kidneys.* Across 19 trials, creatine raised serum creatinine by 0.13 mg/dL (0.07 to 0.18) with no significant difference in urea or estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR; only 8 trials, wide interval) [@Tsiaras2026_creatineKidneyMA]. That pattern fits more creatinine production rather than less filtration: creatine and phosphocreatine cyclise non-enzymatically to creatinine, so a bigger pool makes more creatinine (mechanism). The ISSN position stand describes intakes up to 30 g a day for 5 years as safe and well tolerated in healthy people [@Kreider2017_ISSNcreatine], although few trials last beyond a year.
- *Hair.* The only placebo-controlled trial that measured hair found no effect of 5 g a day for 12 weeks on total or free testosterone, DHT, the DHT:testosterone ratio, hair density or hair thickness [@Lak2025_creatineHairRCT]. It was small and short; the worry traces to one 2009 report of a DHT rise during loading that did not measure hair (background).

!> Stop creatine and get medical advice if you are diagnosed with kidney disease, an eGFR below 60, protein in the urine or diabetic kidney disease, or are prescribed medicines that can harm the kidneys. Tell any doctor who orders blood tests that you take it (see Blood tests below).

sections.title: Caffeine: optional, timed around sleep
sections.body:
**Verdict.** Optional, and besides creatine the one item here with a reliable performance effect. Your current dose of about 100 mg (1.3 mg/kg) is probably below the effective range. If you want the effect, take 150-200 mg at 12:00-12:15 with meal 1 on training days (roughly one and a half to two 250 mL cups of brewed coffee, at the 107 mg per cup assumed in the sleep research below), keep any later dose to 100 mg finished by 17:00-18:00, and take none after 19:00. Staying at 100 mg is also reasonable; just expect little performance effect from it (inference).

**Effect.** The ISSN position stand concludes that 3-6 mg/kg consistently improves performance, that the minimal effective dose may be as low as 2 mg/kg, and that about 9 mg/kg brings frequent side effects without extra benefit. Effects on strength, muscular endurance, movement velocity, sprinting and jumping are small to moderate, aerobic endurance benefits most consistently, the usual timing is 60 min before exercise, and responses vary with caffeine-metabolism genetics and habitual intake [@Guest2021_ISSNcaffeine]. For you, 2 mg/kg is 154 mg, 3 mg/kg is 231 mg and 6 mg/kg is 462 mg.

**Mechanism.** Caffeine reduces sleepiness by blocking [[term:adenosine|adenosine]] receptors [@Reichert2022_adenosineCaffeine], non-selectively at A1 and A2A (background). A 231 mg dose peaks near 4.6 mg/L, about 24 µM, assuming a distribution volume of about 0.65 L/kg (calculation): enough for substantial receptor occupancy, whereas phosphodiesterase inhibition and ryanodine-receptor Ca²⁺ release need roughly 0.1-1 mM, which cannot be reached without toxicity (background pharmacology). Central adenosine blockade is therefore the plausible ergogenic route. It is also what disturbs sleep, because adenosine that accumulates during wakefulness is a signal of sleep pressure [@Reichert2022_adenosineCaffeine].

**The sleep cost on your clock.** In a meta-analysis, caffeine shortened total sleep by 45 min, cut sleep efficiency by 7%, lengthened sleep onset by 9 min, added 12 min of waking after sleep onset and reduced deep (N3/N4) sleep by 11.4 min. To avoid losing total sleep, a 107 mg coffee should come at least 8.8 h before bed and a 217.5 mg pre-workout dose at least 13.2 h before [@Gardiner2023_caffeineSleepMA]. In athletes, caffeine before evening training lowered sleep efficiency by 4.9% (95% CI -7.5 to -2.3; not robust when single studies were removed) and consistently worsened self-rated sleep [@Kocak2025_eveningCaffeineAthletesSleep]. Applied to a 04:00 bedtime, assuming the hours-before-bed rule carries over to a shifted schedule (inference):

| Dose | Latest time as a single dose | Your plan |
|---|---|---|
| About 200 mg | 14:45 | 12:00-12:15, 16 h before bed |
| About 100 mg | 19:10 | Finished by 17:00-18:00 |

Two doses add up. With a half-life of 5-8 h (background), 200 mg at 12:00 leaves about 22-50 mg in your body at 04:00, and a further 100 mg adds about 29-46 mg if taken at 19:00 or 22-39 mg if taken at 17:00 (calculation, first-order elimination). That is why the second dose stops by 17:00-18:00, earlier than the single-dose rule allows. Late caffeine also delays the [[term:circadian-rhythm|circadian clock]] (background), which you do not need on an already late schedule.

**Limits and cautions**

- Count every source: coffee, tea and chai at the work break, colas, energy drinks and pre-workout products. Chai at 19:30-20:00 breaks the 19:00 rule.
- Brewed and instant coffee vary in caffeine. Using the same product and measure each day keeps the dose consistent; a caffeine tablet, where available, gives a known dose (practical convention).
- Stay under 400 mg a day and 200 mg per dose (EFSA reference values; background).
- Lower the dose or stop if you get palpitations, anxiety, reflux or blood pressure above about 130/80 mmHg. Some medicines, for example fluvoxamine and ciprofloxacin, slow caffeine clearance (background).
- If falling asleep at 04:00 takes more than about 30 min, or sleep feels worse, drop the second dose first, then halve the pre-training dose. Log caffeine times in your sleep diary ([[plan:sleep]]).
- If your training time moves later, re-anchor: a dose of about 200 mg needs at least 13 h before bedtime, or drop it.

sections.title: L-theanine: optional
sections.body:
**Verdict.** Optional. It does nothing known for muscle or fat loss, so dropping it costs nothing measurable. Keep 100-200 mg with the 12:00 caffeine only if you value how the combination feels.

**Evidence.** Compared with placebo, theanine plus caffeine produced small acute improvements within 1-2 h in digit-vigilance accuracy (SMD 0.20, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.38) and attention-switching accuracy (0.33, 0.13 to 0.54), while the intervals for choice reaction time (-0.48, -1.01 to 0.05) and mood (0.26, -0.10 to 0.63) included zero; theanine alone shortened choice reaction time slightly (-0.35, -0.61 to -0.10). Two of the review's authors are employed by a tea company [@Payne2025_theanineMA]. An earlier meta-analysis found moderate effects of the combination on alertness and attention switching, with the effect size tracking the caffeine dose more than the theanine dose [@Camfield2014_theanineCaffeineMA]. No reviewed trial compared theanine plus caffeine with caffeine alone, measured training outcomes or showed that theanine offsets caffeine's sleep costs.

**Mechanism.** L-theanine (N⁵-ethyl-L-glutamine), a glutamine analogue from tea, crosses the blood-brain barrier on the large neutral amino-acid transporter LAT1. It binds glutamate receptors only weakly, raises brain GABA, dopamine and serotonin in rodents, and at 50-200 mg increases resting alpha-band EEG activity in humans (background). It might take the edge off caffeine's arousal, but it does not undo adenosine-receptor blockade, so it is no licence for later caffeine (inference).

**Diet and safety.** Tea supplies theanine together with caffeine (background). Doses of 100-400 mg a day are well tolerated in trials (background). Do not use it as a sleep aid.

sections.title: Magnesium glycinate: optional trial
sections.body:
**Verdict.** Optional, and only as a 4-week trial. Your training does not require it.

**Evidence**

- *Sleep.* Three small trials in older adults with insomnia, all at moderate-to-high risk of bias, found sleep onset 17 min faster than with placebo (95% CI -27 to -7 min) and no significant change in total sleep (+16 min), with [[term:grade|GRADE certainty]] low to very low [@Mah2021_magnesiumInsomniaMA]. You are not that population.
- *Cramps.* In a Cochrane review, magnesium did not reduce idiopathic cramps (weekly cramps -9.6%, 95% CI -23.1 to 4.0, moderate certainty; responders RR 1.04, 0.84 to 1.29, high certainty). No trial has tested exercise-associated cramps, and minor, mostly gastrointestinal adverse events were about 50% more frequent (RR 1.51, 0.98 to 2.33) [@Garrison2020_magnesiumCrampsCochrane].
- *Performance.* No reviewed source shows that magnesium improves strength, growth or recovery in adults who are not deficient. That is a gap in the evidence, not proof of no effect.

**Mechanism.** Most intracellular magnesium exists as Mg-ATP, the true substrate of myosin ATPase, SERCA, Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and creatine kinase, which is why deficiency impairs muscle. In replete people, extracellular Mg²⁺ is tightly regulated and cerebrospinal-fluid magnesium changes little with oral supplements, so the proposed sleep routes (NMDA-receptor block, GABA-A modulation) are plausible mainly in deficiency (background physiology; inference).

**Read the label.** The upper limit for magnesium from supplements is 350 mg of elemental magnesium a day (background). Fully reacted magnesium bisglycinate is about 14% magnesium by mass (24.3 of 172.4 g/mol), so ‘500 mg magnesium glycinate’ may mean only about 70 mg of magnesium unless the label states elemental content; ‘buffered’ products mixed with magnesium oxide contain more (calculation). 200 mg of elemental magnesium as bisglycinate is about 1.4 g of compound, carrying about 1.2 g of glycine (calculation).

**Trial protocol.** Take 100-200 mg of elemental magnesium with meal 4 (01:30-02:00) for 4 weeks while keeping your sleep diary ([[plan:sleep]]). Continue only if sleep onset or quality is clearly better, and stop at once if your stools loosen. Food covers most needs: dal and other pulses, nuts and seeds, whole grains and millets, and leafy greens (inference).

!> Do not take magnesium supplements if your kidney function is reduced. Long-term proton-pump inhibitors or diuretics, or chronic diarrhoea, are reasons to ask a doctor to check your magnesium. Take magnesium 2-4 h apart from tetracycline or quinolone antibiotics and bisphosphonates, whose absorption it reduces (background).

sections.title: Vitamin D3: keep at 1,000 IU
sections.body:
**Verdict.** Keep 1,000 IU (25 µg) a day with meal 2.

**Why you.** In pooled Indian studies, 67% of adults were deficient (95% CI 61 to 73%) and the mean 25-hydroxyvitamin D, 25(OH)D, across South Asian studies was about 19 ng/mL, with higher prevalence in women than men [@Siddiqee2021_SouthAsiaVitDPrevalence]; a broader Indian meta-analysis gave 61% [@Venkatesh2021_IndiaMicronutrientDeficiency]. Your day adds risk. Skin makes vitamin D only under UVB (290-315 nm), which is strong mainly from late morning to mid-afternoon, does not pass through window glass and is used less efficiently by darker skin (background physiology). You are indoors at 13:00-14:05 and from 16:00 to 01:00, so 12:00-16:00 outdoors is your only realistic window (inference), and few foods supply much vitamin D (background).

**What it will and will not do.** In healthy 18-40-year-olds, supplements raised upper- and lower-limb strength slightly (both SMD 0.32; lower limb 95% CI 0.01 to 0.63) [@Tomlinson2014_vitDStrengthMA]; the benefit probably depends on correcting a deficiency (inference). The Endocrine Society's 2024 guideline suggests against empiric doses above the Dietary Reference Intake to prevent disease in healthy adults under 75, and against routine 25(OH)D testing, including in people with darker skin; it finds no clear evidence for an optimal 25(OH)D target [@Demay2024_EndoSocVitDGuideline]. Large prevention trials of 2,000 IU a day did not reduce cancer or cardiovascular events (background). So 1,000 IU a day is a judgement: modestly above the 600 IU reference intake because your deficiency risk is high, and far below the 4,000 IU upper limit (both background values).

**Mechanism.** Cholecalciferol is 25-hydroxylated in the liver, mainly by CYP2R1 in a substrate-driven, weakly regulated step, so 25(OH)D tracks supply; its half-life of about 2-3 weeks means about 3 months to reach a new steady state. Renal CYP27B1 makes calcitriol under tight PTH and FGF23 control, so calcitriol is often normal even in moderate deficiency and is useless as a status marker (background physiology). Vitamin D is fat-soluble, so take it with a meal that contains fat (practical convention).

**If your product is 60,000 IU.** Sachets and capsules of 60,000 IU are widely used in India (inference). Taken weekly, they average about 8,600 IU a day, above the upper limit: a time-limited treatment course, not maintenance. Continue only if a doctor prescribed it for a documented deficiency, for a stated period. Otherwise switch to 1,000 IU daily; a single 60,000 IU dose is 15 times the daily upper limit, so do not use these products for self-directed maintenance.

**Sunlight.** Where practical, spend 10-20 min outdoors between 12:00 and 15:00 with face and arms uncovered (inference); it doubles as the bright light your sleep plan uses after waking ([[plan:sleep]]). Sunlight cannot cause vitamin D toxicity, because prolonged UVB converts previtamin D3 to inactive photoproducts (background). In the hottest months keep exposures short and drink enough water.

!> Stop vitamin D and see a doctor if you are diagnosed with high blood calcium, kidney stones or a granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis.

sections.title: Vitamin K2: remove
sections.body:
**Verdict.** Stop it, unless a doctor prescribed it. If your vitamin D3 comes combined with K2, the K2 is harmless at usual doses for someone not taking anticoagulants, so finish the pack and buy plain D3 next time (background; inference).

**Evidence.** Markers of functional vitamin K insufficiency (uncarboxylated osteocalcin, and dephospho-uncarboxylated matrix Gla protein, dp-ucMGP) cluster in children and in adults from about 40, and supplement responses were largest in those with the poorest status; the authors named children and adults over 40 as target groups [@Theuwissen2014_vitKStatusHealthy]. The trials behind K2's reputation used surrogate markers in other populations: menaquinone-7 (MK-7) at 180 µg a day for 3 years halved dp-ucMGP and reduced arterial stiffness in postmenopausal women [@Knapen2015_MK7ArterialStiffness], and MK-7 improved carboxylation dose-dependently in haemodialysis patients [@Westenfeld2011_MK7DoseCarboxylation]. No reviewed trial reports clinical outcomes in healthy young men.

**The ‘D3 needs K2’ argument.** Vitamin K hydroquinone is the cofactor of γ-glutamyl carboxylase, which activates osteocalcin and matrix Gla protein, and calcitriol up-regulates both proteins, so high vitamin D intakes could raise carboxylation demand (mechanism). At 1,000 IU a day the extra demand is small, and no trial shows harm from modest vitamin D without K2 (inference); the Endocrine Society keeps healthy adults near the reference intake in any case [@Demay2024_EndoSocVitDGuideline]. Leafy greens supply vitamin K1, and eggs, dairy and fermented foods supply some K2 (background).

!> Never take any form of vitamin K with warfarin or acenocoumarol without medical advice. These drugs block vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), so changing your vitamin K intake changes their effect.

sections.title: Omega-3: optional, fish first
sections.body:
**Verdict.** Optional. Prefer fish: two oily-fish meals a week, such as sardine or mackerel (Indian oil sardine is sold as mathi or chaala, Indian mackerel as bangda or ayala), and then stop the capsule. If you eat oily fish less often, keep a supplement supplying 250-500 mg EPA+DHA a day with meal 2. Do not expect extra muscle, and do not take high doses ‘for recovery’.

**Evidence.** Omega-3 does not add muscle mass to resistance training: a meta-analysis of 4 trials found no effect on muscle mass while reporting improved strength [@Uchida2024_omega3RT_MA]. In a 10-week trial in young adults, fish oil raised blood EPA+DHA by 110% but lean-mass gains were similar (+3.4% vs +2.4%, p = 0.46); [[term:1rm|one-repetition maximum (1RM)]] bench press rose more (+17.7% vs +9.7%, p = 0.047) while absolute squat did not differ, among several uncorrected outcomes and with 25% dropout [@Heileson2023_fishOilRTyoungRCT]. In older adults, grip strength did not change significantly (SMD 0.61, 95% CI -0.05 to 1.27; [[term:i2|I²]] 90%) [@Timraz2023_omega3StrengthOlderMA]. A strength benefit is possible but fragile.

**Mechanism.** EPA (20:5n-3) and DHA (22:6n-3) are incorporated into membrane phospholipids over weeks, changing membrane order and raft composition. In older adults, about 4 g a day increased the [[term:mps|muscle protein synthesis (MPS)]] response to amino acids and insulin, but results in younger adults are inconsistent (background), which fits the null results for muscle mass.

**Limits.** In cardiovascular-outcome trials in older adults, omega-3 supplements were associated with more atrial fibrillation, more so above 1 g a day (background, not among the reviewed sources); hence the 1 g ceiling. A capsule labelled ‘1,000 mg fish oil’ often contains only about 300 mg of EPA+DHA, so read the EPA and DHA lines (background). Freshwater carp such as rohu supply much less EPA+DHA than oily sea fish (background).

!> Stop the supplement and see a doctor if you develop palpitations or are diagnosed with atrial fibrillation. Fasting triglycerides of 150 mg/dL or more call for medical review, not self-dosing.

sections.title: Vitamin B12: keep a modest dose
sections.body:
**Verdict.** Keep 250-500 µg a day with meal 2, or 1,000 µg three times a week, as low-cost insurance.

**Why.** Vitamin B12 deficiency was found in 53% (95% CI 41 to 64%) of people tested in pooled Indian studies, and folate deficiency in 37% [@Venkatesh2021_IndiaMicronutrientDeficiency]. Those estimates mix ages and diets and give no figure for omnivorous men; eating milk or curd, eggs, meat or fish every day usually meets the adult requirement of 2.4 µg a day (inference; background reference value).

**Mechanism and dose.** Food B12 is released by gastric acid and pepsin, binds haptocorrin and then intrinsic factor, and is taken up through the cubilin-amnionless receptor in the terminal ileum, a route that saturates at about 1.5-2 µg per meal. About 1% of any oral dose also crosses passively, independent of intrinsic factor, so 500 µg supplies about 5 µg, several times the requirement, even if the intrinsic-factor route works poorly (background physiology). Cyanocobalamin and methylcobalamin both work (inference). B12 has no established upper limit, so the common 1,500 µg methylcobalamin tablets are not harmful, but 2-3 a week are plenty (inference).

**When you could drop it.** When a serum B12 with methylmalonic acid or holotranscobalamin is normal and you eat animal foods every day (see Blood tests below).

!> Keep taking it and see a doctor if you use a proton-pump inhibitor or metformin, have gastritis, or notice numbness, tingling or unsteadiness.

sections.title: Folic acid: remove
sections.body:
**Verdict.** Stop it, unless a doctor prescribed it; in that case continue as prescribed and ask whether your B12 status was checked first.

**Why.** No reviewed source shows a benefit of folic acid supplements, for training or anything else, in a man who is not deficient. Your diet supplies food folate from dal and other pulses, leafy greens and eggs. The upper limit for synthetic folic acid is 1,000 µg a day (background; food folate does not count), and the 5 mg tablets common in India are five times that (inference about local products).

**Masking: the methyl-folate trap.** Methionine synthase uses methylcobalamin to transfer the methyl group of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate to homocysteine, regenerating methionine and tetrahydrofolate. Because the MTHFR reaction that forms 5-methyl-THF is effectively irreversible in vivo, B12 deficiency traps folate as 5-methyl-THF, thymidylate synthesis falters and red-cell precursors become megaloblastic. Synthetic folic acid enters the pool through dihydrofolate reductase, bypassing the trap, so it corrects the anaemia while the B12-dependent neurological damage continues (background biochemistry). With B12 deficiency found in about half of people tested in India [@Venkatesh2021_IndiaMicronutrientDeficiency], unneeded folic acid carries a real risk of hiding it.

sections.title: Whey protein: optional, as food
sections.body:
**Verdict.** Optional, and simply food. Buy it only if it closes a protein gap that home-cooked meals do not, at a cost per gram of protein you accept. Your nutrition plan can reach 140-155 g a day without it, using the whey-free meal 1 swap ([[plan:nutrition]]).

**Evidence.** Protein supplements added to resistance training increased fat-free mass by 0.30 kg (95% CI 0.09 to 0.52) and 1RM strength by 2.49 kg (0.64 to 4.33), with the benefit flattening at about 1.6 g/kg a day of total protein [@Morton2018_proteinRT]: the effect comes from extra protein, not from powder as such. Soy and animal-protein supplements produced similar gains [@Messina2018_soy]. Whey is rich in [[term:leucine|leucine]] (about 10% of its protein; background), the amino acid that activates [[term:mtorc1|mTORC1]] through Sestrin2 and the Rag GTPases (background), and after whole-body training 40 g of whey raised MPS about 20% more than 20 g [@Macnaughton2016_20v40].

**Quality of Indian products.** Independent testing of popular protein supplements sold in India found that most missed their labelled protein content (some exceeded it, suggesting amino-acid spiking), major brands contained aflatoxins and pesticide residues, many contained lead and arsenic, some contained potentially liver-toxic herbal extracts (green tea extract, turmeric, Garcinia cambogia, ashwagandha), and Indian-made products did worse than multinational ones [@Philips2024_CitizensProteinProject]. A follow-up of 34 whey products found that mainstream sports whey powders averaged 75.6 g protein per 100 g, close to their labels, with 94% above 60 g per 100 g; pharmacy-sold ‘medical’ protein powders averaged 29.1 g per 100 g, 83% were mislabelled by more than 5%, 44% contained at least 2 g sugar per 100 g and 89% were spiked with taurine [@Philips2025_CitizensProteinProject2].

Why spiking pays: label protein is usually total nitrogen (Kjeldahl or Dumas) × 6.38 for dairy, so each gram of taurine (11.2% N) reads as about 0.71 g of protein, glycine (18.7% N) as about 1.19 g and creatine (32% N) as about 2 g, all far cheaper than whey (calculation). Protein calculated from the amino-acid profile exposes it.

**If you buy** (criteria inferred from the testing above)

- A mainstream sports whey concentrate or isolate, not a pharmacy ‘medical’ protein.
- At least 70 g protein per 100 g on the label, with an amino-acid profile showing leucine at about 10% of protein.
- No herbal extracts, no ‘proprietary blend’ and no added free amino acids such as taurine, glycine or creatine.
- A batch-specific certificate of analysis from an independent accredited laboratory covering protein, heavy metals and aflatoxins.
- If milk disagrees with you, isolate or soy protein.
- Cost: roughly INR 2,000-3,000 a month for one scoop a day at 2024-25 prices (inference); compare cost per 10 g of protein with eggs, soya chunks and milk first.

sections.title: Ashwagandha: avoid
sections.body:
**Verdict.** Do not add it, alone or in blends. It is not in your stack; make sure it does not arrive inside a protein powder, ‘testosterone booster’ or sleep or stress product (look for Withania somnifera on the label).

**Benefit.** A three-level meta-analysis of 13 trials (599 participants) found a moderate pooled effect on exercise performance (Hedges g 0.47, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.69; I² 60%), but the 95% prediction interval (-0.40 to 1.33) crosses zero. Aerobic endurance was the most consistent outcome (g 0.54), strength effects were positive but uncertain, and 500-600 mg a day of extract was most studied [@Li2026_ashwagandhaPerformanceMA]. An earlier Bayesian meta-analysis was also favourable [@Bonilla2021_ashwagandhaBayesianMA]. Trials are small and extracts differ.

**Harm.** Ashwagandha causes idiosyncratic, mostly cholestatic liver injury. In an Indian multicentre series, injury occurred with single-ingredient products free of adulterants; of 8 such patients, 5 had pre-existing chronic liver disease and 3 developed acute-on-chronic liver failure and died [@Philips2023_ashwagandhaHILI_India]. In Iceland and the US, jaundice appeared 2-12 weeks after starting, itching lasted 5-20 weeks and liver tests normalised within 1-5 months, without liver failure [@Bjornsson2020_ashwagandhaDILI]. Indian testing has found it added to protein supplements [@Philips2024_CitizensProteinProject]. Incidence is unknown and no dose-response has been shown; inhibition of the bile-salt export pump by withanolides is one candidate mechanism (theoretical). A modest, uncertain benefit does not justify an unpredictable risk to your liver (judgement).

!!> If you have taken ashwagandha and notice dark urine, yellowing of the eyes or skin, itching all over or pain under the right ribs, stop it and get liver tests promptly.

sections.title: Other products: do not add
sections.body:
These are the products most often suggested to new lifters. None is worth your money for your goals.

- **HMB (β-hydroxy-β-methylbutyrate).** An independent meta-analysis in young adults doing resistance training found no effect on fat-free mass, fat mass or strength, only a small effect on total body mass [@Jakubowski2020_HMByoungMA]. The ISSN position stand is more positive, mainly for untrained people, at about 38 mg/kg a day (2.9 g for you), but it pools no data and its authors have commercial ties [@Rathmacher2024_ISSNHMB]. Only about 5% of leucine's keto acid (α-ketoisocaproate) becomes HMB, so making 3 g would take about 60 g of leucine (background biochemistry); your dietary protein already drives mTORC1 signalling through leucine itself (inference).
- **Beta-alanine.** It raises muscle carnosine, an intracellular H⁺ buffer (imidazole pKa about 6.8), which helps where acid accumulation limits efforts of roughly 0.5-10 min; hypertrophy sets of 20-60 s with full rest gain little (mechanism; background). It also causes harmless tingling at larger single doses (background).
- **Dietary nitrate (beetroot juice) and citrulline.** Nitrate is mainly an endurance aid and citrulline's acute strength effects are small at most; neither has shown added muscle growth (background, not among the reviewed sources).
- **BCAA or EAA drinks.** Your 140-155 g of daily protein already supplies these amino acids in larger amounts (inference).
- **Melatonin.** Not routinely. It is a weak hypnotic whose main action is shifting circadian timing, which a stable 04:00-12:00 schedule does not need (background). Protect sleep first with a dark, cool, quiet room, dim light from about 01:00, bright light after 12:00 and the caffeine cut-offs ([[plan:sleep]], [[dec:D22]]). Persistent insomnia or a rotating shift pattern is a reason for medical review, where melatonin may have a place.
- **Multi-ingredient pre-workouts, fat burners and ‘testosterone boosters’.** They combine undisclosed or high caffeine doses with herbal extracts of the kind found in Indian protein products [@Philips2024_CitizensProteinProject], and their ingredients cannot be checked against upper limits (inference).

sections.title: Blood tests worth considering
sections.body:
No blood test is needed because of your supplements. If you have tests for another reason, these are the results your stack affects and what would change. The vitamin D thresholds are background reference values, not from the reviewed sources.

| Test | When it is worth doing | What the result changes |
|---|---|---|
| Serum creatinine and eGFR | Any routine panel | Expect creatinine about 0.13 mg/dL higher on creatine (95% CI 0.07 to 0.18) [@Tsiaras2026_creatineKidneyMA]. For you, a rise from 0.90 to 1.03 mg/dL would lower the creatinine-based eGFR from about 117 to about 100 mL/min/1.73 m² (calculation, CKD-EPI 2021). Tell the clinician you take creatine; if kidney function is genuinely in question, ask for a cystatin C-based eGFR. A large meat meal the day before also raises creatinine (background). |
| Vitamin B12 with methylmalonic acid (MMA) or holotranscobalamin | Optional, once; sooner with numbness, tingling, unusual fatigue, or proton-pump inhibitor or metformin use | Serum B12 alone is insensitive (background). Normal B12 and MMA with daily animal foods: you may drop the B12 tablet. Low B12 or raised MMA: medical treatment and a search for the cause. |
| 25(OH)D | Not routinely [@Demay2024_EndoSocVitDGuideline]; only when a doctor has a clinical reason | Below 12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L): doctor-directed repletion. 12-20 ng/mL: keep 1,000 IU a day, add midday sun and ask whether a short course is warranted (inference). 20-50 ng/mL: no change. Above 50 ng/mL (125 nmol/L): reduce or stop. |
| Folate | Only with anaemia or another clinical reason, and always alongside B12 | Folic acid is justified only for documented folate deficiency after B12 deficiency has been excluded. |
| Liver tests (ALT, ALP, bilirubin) | If jaundice, dark urine or itching follows any herbal product | Stop the product and follow medical advice. |
| Fasting lipids | With routine health checks | Triglycerides of 150 mg/dL or more: medical review rather than self-dosed fish oil. |
| Blood pressure | If you raise your caffeine dose | Above about 130/80 mmHg: lower or stop caffeine and see a doctor. |
| Serum magnesium | Only with a clinical reason | Less than 1% of body magnesium is in serum, so a normal value says little about status (background). |

Indian laboratories usually report 25(OH)D in ng/mL; multiply by 2.5 for nmol/L. Symptoms that need prompt attention, whatever their cause, are listed in [[plan:safety]].

sections.title: Buying and quality
sections.body:
No reviewed source evaluates supplement certification schemes in the Indian market, so these rules are practical convention informed by the Indian product testing above.

1. **Single ingredients with a stated dose.** Plain creatine monohydrate; cholecalciferol (IU per tablet); cyanocobalamin or methylcobalamin (µg); magnesium (mg of elemental magnesium); fish oil (mg of EPA plus DHA). Single-ingredient products are the only way to check doses against upper limits.
2. **FSSAI licence number.** Supplements sold in India should carry the 14-digit licence number of the business from the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (background). It shows the business is licensed; it does not show that your batch was tested for content or contaminants (inference).
3. **No blends.** Avoid proprietary blends, pre-workouts, fat burners and ‘testosterone boosters’, especially those containing green tea extract, Garcinia, turmeric extracts or ashwagandha, all of which turned up in Indian protein products [@Philips2024_CitizensProteinProject].
4. **Batch certificates for powders.** Prefer a certificate of analysis for your batch from an independent accredited laboratory (in India, usually NABL-accredited; background) that reports protein as an amino-acid profile, heavy metals and aflatoxins, and match the batch number on the tub.
5. **Sport-certification marks.** Schemes such as Informed Sport, Informed Choice or NSF Certified for Sport mainly screen batches for substances banned in sport. Check each scheme's website for what it covers: it may not include protein content, heavy metals or aflatoxins (inference).
6. **Where to buy.** The brand's own store or authorised sellers; check seals, batch numbers and expiry dates, and distrust prices far below the market (practical convention).
7. **A pharmacy is not a quality mark.** Pharmacy-sold ‘medical’ protein powders performed worst in Indian testing [@Philips2025_CitizensProteinProject2].

+> When you buy a new product, photograph the label and note the brand, the dose per unit and the batch number. It makes the upper-limit checks, and any later question from a doctor, quick to answer.

pages.title: Sleep and circadian plan
pages.tagline: A fixed 04:00-12:00 night, a dark daytime bedroom, and light, caffeine and food timed to your own clock.
pages.summary: Your sleep is already long enough: about 8 hours in bed from 04:00 to 12:00. The plan is to protect it rather than move it. Keep the same bed and wake times every day, days off included, because in a large cohort regular timing predicted mortality more strongly than sleep duration did, and a late but fixed schedule avoids the misalignment that comes from shifting sleep at weekends. Sunrise falls inside your night, so the bedroom has to be properly dark, quiet and cool. Light, caffeine, food and exercise are timed against your clock, not the conventional one: bright light soon after waking, dim light from 01:00, caffeine before training, at most one later dose of about 100 mg finished by 17:00-18:00 and none after about 19:00, your last proper meal finished by about 02:00, and no hard training after about 02:00. Your 13:00 session falls in your biological morning, so it gets a full warm-up. Track sleep with a one-minute diary and a questionnaire every 4-8 weeks, and treat a wearable's sleep score with caution. Persistent insomnia is treated first with CBT-I, not pills or supplements; loud snoring with daytime sleepiness needs a doctor.

sections.title: Your schedule
sections.body:
**Keep 04:00-12:00, every day.** Go to bed at 04:00 and get up at 12:00 on work days and days off alike, within about ±30 minutes (practical convention; see [[dec:D22]]). Eight hours in bed usually yields about 7-7.5 hours of actual sleep, because some time in bed is always spent awake (inference). The adult consensus is at least 7 hours a night on a regular basis; more than 9 hours may suit young adults, people recovering from sleep debt and people who are ill [@Watson2015_sleepDurationConsensus].

**Why regularity matters more than clock time.** In a large cohort with wrist accelerometers, the four more regular quintiles of a sleep-regularity index had 20-48% lower all-cause mortality than the least regular quintile, and regularity predicted mortality more strongly than sleep duration [@Windred2024_sleepRegularityMortality]. Shifting your sleep between work days and days off ([[term:social-jetlag|social jetlag]]) is associated with slightly higher BMI and waist in observational studies (BMI r 0.12; waist r 0.15) [@Arab2023_socialJetlagObesityMA], although one meta-analysis found no link with metabolic syndrome or diabetes and rated its evidence low [@Bouman2022_socialJetlagMetabolicMA]. Evening types ([[term:chronotype|chronotype]]) have slightly higher mortality than morning types (HR 1.10, 95% CI 1.02-1.18), possibly partly through residual confounding and, as the authors propose, through forcing a late body clock into early work and social schedules [@Knutson2018_chronotypeMortality]. A late schedule that never shifts avoids most of that misalignment, so for you the risk to manage is irregularity, not lateness (inference).

**Should you move it earlier?** Not required. In one small randomised trial, night owls who advanced their sleep by about 2 hours, using earlier fixed wake times, morning light, fixed meals and caffeine timing, reported less depression and stress and had better morning reaction time and grip strength [@FacerChilds2019_nightOwlPhaseAdvance]; their work did not end at 01:00, though. Because your shift ends at 01:00 and meal 4 should finish about 2 hours before bed, the most you could advance is about 30 minutes (03:30-11:30), and only if meal 4 can end by about 01:30 and your diary still shows at least 7 hours of sleep; otherwise keep 04:00-12:00 (inference).

**Why it matters for your goals.**
