- Muscle: after one night without sleep, [[term:mps|muscle protein synthesis (MPS)]] measured the next afternoon was 18% lower, cortisol 21% higher and testosterone 24% lower in a small crossover trial [@Lamon2021_sleepDeprivationMPS]. Growth-hormone secretion tracks the amount of slow-wave sleep [@VanCauter2000_SWS_GH], although no source here shows that sleep-related growth-hormone pulses matter for muscle growth.
- Performance: acute sleep loss (6 hours or less in 24) reduced exercise performance by about 7.6% on average (95% CI 3.1-11.9%), strength included [@Craven2022_sleepLossPerformanceMA].
- Fat loss (small trials in overweight adults): during 14 days of dieting, 5.5 rather than 8.5 hours in bed cut fat loss from 1.4 to 0.6 kg and raised fat-free-mass loss from 1.5 to 2.4 kg [@Nedeltcheva2010_sleepCaloricRestriction]. Even about 1 hour less sleep on 5 nights a week, with catch-up sleep on the other 2, lowered the share of weight lost as fat [@Wang2018_sleepRestrictionWeightLoss].

+> **Fat-loss rule.** In a fat-loss block, treat at least 7 hours of sleep as part of the diet. If you sleep less than about 6.5 hours on several nights in a week, shrink or pause the deficit until sleep recovers (the 6.5-hour trigger is practical convention). See [[rule:energy-adjustment]] and [[rule:phase-nutrition]].

**If a night is cut short.**

| Situation | What to do |
|---|---|
| You have to lose sleep | Go to bed later and keep the 12:00 wake, rather than waking early. Total sleep deprivation and waking earlier than normal consistently impaired performance; going to bed later did not consistently do so [@Craven2022_sleepLossPerformanceMA]. |
| One short night | Train as planned. Morning tasks were largely unaffected by prior sleep loss [@Craven2022_sleepLossPerformanceMA], and your 13:00 session falls early in your waking day (inference). |
| Several short nights in a row | Keep training but ease off: drop the last set of each exercise or keep one more [[term:rir|rep in reserve (RIR)]], and prioritise recovery sleep (inference). In a small laboratory study in young men, five nights at 4 hours in bed impaired glucose tolerance, mitochondrial function and sarcoplasmic protein synthesis; interval exercise during the restriction prevented those changes [@Saner2020_sleepRestrictionHIIE] but not the worse mood and alertness [@Saner2023_sleepRestrictionMoodAlertness]. |

**More than 8 hours?** Sprint times and shooting accuracy improved after sleep extension in an uncontrolled study of 11 college basketball players [@Mah2011_sleepExtensionBasketball], and extension and naps were the most effective sleep interventions in a review of athletes [@Cunha2023_sleepInterventionsAthletes], but these are small, low-certainty studies in athletes. If you already sleep 7-8 hours, there is no need to chase 9 (inference). The underlying science is in [[sci:sci-sleep]].

sections.title: Bedroom for daytime sleep
sections.body:
Sunrise falls inside your sleep window (roughly 05:30-07:00 across India, depending on place and season; approximate), so most of your night is spent in daylight unless the room is sealed against it.

| Factor | Target | How |
|---|---|---|
| Darkness | As dark as possible: 1 lux melanopic EDI or less at the eye (expert consensus) [@Brown2022_lightRecommendations] | Blackout curtains or blackout film with the edges closed; a contoured eye mask as well or instead; tape over standby LEDs |
| Noise | No sudden noise | Foam earplugs, or steady background sound (fan, white-noise app); ask the household to keep 04:00-12:00 quiet |
| Temperature | Cool enough that you neither sweat nor need heavy covers | Air conditioning or a fan and light cotton bedding; with air conditioning, about 24-26 °C is a common starting point (practical convention; no study gives a target) |
| Phone | No light or alerts during sleep | Do Not Disturb from 04:00 to 12:00 with emergency contacts allowed; screen face down or across the room; one alarm at 12:00 |

**Darkness.** One night of sleep under 100 lux room light, compared with under 3 lux, raised night-time heart rate, lowered heart-rate variability and increased next-morning insulin resistance in a laboratory study [@Mason2022_lightDuringSleep]. In more than 88,000 people who wore light sensors for a week, the brightest nights were associated with 21-34% higher mortality (adjusted HR 1.21-1.34) [@Windred2024_lightExposureMortality]. One study is small and the other observational, but both point the same way as the consensus threshold.

**Masks and earplugs.** In a systematic review, mostly of intensive-care patients, eye masks and earplugs improved subjective sleep quality; objective benefits were not shown [@Locihova2017_earplugsEyeMask]. They are cheap and harmless, so they are worth a trial (inference).

**Heat.** With normal bedding, heat increases wakefulness and reduces slow-wave and REM sleep, and humid heat adds to the load [@OkamotoMizuno2012_thermalEnvironment]. A room that warms up after sunrise can therefore cost you deep sleep in the second half of your night; an air-conditioner timer that keeps cooling until 12:00 avoids this (inference).

**Phone.** In the few studies in athletes, removing electronic devices at night did not change sleep or performance [@Cunha2023_sleepInterventionsAthletes]. The aim is to keep light and notifications out of your sleep, not to give up the phone.

sections.title: Light plan for your clock
sections.body:
**Mechanism.** Light sets your [[term:circadian-rhythm|circadian clock]] mainly through [[term:melanopsin|melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs)]], which respond most to short-wavelength (blue-cyan) light. Their effects are predicted better by melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melanopic EDI) than by ordinary lux [@Brown2022_lightRecommendations]. The clock itself is a transcription-translation feedback loop: CLOCK-BMAL1 drives transcription of its own repressors, the PER-CRY complex, which gives a roughly 24-hour cycle that times much of metabolism [@Laothamatas2023_clockMechanism]. Evening light also suppresses melatonin (standard physiology).

**The thresholds.** An expert consensus recommends, measured at eye level: at least 250 lux melanopic EDI during the day, preferably from daylight; no more than 10 lux from at least 3 hours before bedtime; and no more than 1 lux during sleep (10 lux if you need to see) [@Brown2022_lightRecommendations]. The thresholds were written for conventional daytime schedules, explicitly not for shift workers, so mapping them onto your day is inference.

| Time | Your biological time | Light target | How |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12:00-14:00 | Early morning | Bright light soon after waking, ideally outdoor daylight | Open the curtains at 12:00; walk at least part of the way to the gym outdoors, or spend 10-20 minutes outside (durations are practical, not evidence-derived) |
| 14:00-16:00 | Late morning | Daylight when practical | Eat meal 2 near a window; walk after it ([[plan:activity]]) |
| 16:00-01:00 | Day | Keep the workspace bright | Bright overhead light plus a desk lamp; sit facing a window until dusk |
| 01:00-04:00 | Evening, the last 3 hours before bed | 10 lux or less | Dim, warm lamps at home; phone and laptop at minimum brightness with night mode; no bright overhead light during meal 4 |
| 04:00-12:00 | Night | 1 lux or less | See the bedroom section; a dim, warm night light for bathroom trips |

Outdoor daylight, even in shade, is usually far brighter than indoor lighting (general physics), which is why a short time outside does more than a well-lit room. In a cohort with personal light sensors, the brightest days were associated with lower mortality (adjusted HR 0.66-0.83 in the top decile versus the darkest half) and the brightest nights with higher mortality; both early and late modelled circadian timing also predicted higher risk [@Windred2024_lightExposureMortality]. Bright light early in your day anchors the clock where it is, and dim evenings stop it drifting later (inference). If falling asleep at 04:00 becomes harder, check your evening light first.

sections.title: Caffeine plan
sections.body:
**Mechanism.** [[term:adenosine|Adenosine]] is an endogenous sleep-regulating signal tied to sleep pressure. Caffeine reduces sleepiness by antagonising adenosine receptors, and the same action delays and lightens sleep when it is taken too late [@Reichert2022_adenosineCaffeine].

**Size of the effect.** Across 24 studies, caffeine reduced total sleep by about 45 minutes and sleep efficiency by 7%, lengthened the time to fall asleep by 9 minutes and night waking by 12 minutes, and cut deep (N3) sleep by about 11 minutes [@Gardiner2023_caffeineSleepMA]. The same analysis modelled how long before bed a dose must be taken to avoid losing total sleep.

| Dose | Example | Gap before bed (model) | Latest time with a 04:00 bedtime |
|---|---|---|---|
| About 100 mg (107 mg in the model) | One 250 mL cup of brewed coffee; a 100 mg caffeine tablet | 8.8 hours | About 19:00 (model: 19:12) |
| About 200 mg (217.5 mg in the model) | A typical pre-workout serving, or two coffees together | 13.2 hours | About 14:45 (model: 14:48) |

**Your plan.**

- Caffeine at about 12:00-12:30, before training, is 15.5-16 hours before bed and fits both limits. Caffeine was also one of the strategies that reduced time-of-day differences in performance [@Kusumoto2021_diurnal_variation], which suits a session early in your day.
- During the shift, keep any further caffeine (coffee, tea, cola, energy drinks) to one dose of about 100 mg, finished by 17:00-18:00, and take none after about 19:00. After that, switch to decaffeinated drinks or water.
- The cut-offs are model estimates for an average person and a single dose. Two doses in a day add up, and sensitivity varies between people (inference). If your diary shows you often take more than 30 minutes to fall asleep, drop the second dose first, then halve the pre-training dose (practical convention).
- Record caffeine times in the sleep diary. Dose and safety are covered in [[plan:supplements]] and [[dec:D21]].

sections.title: Exercise timing
sections.body:
Your 13:00 session ends about 14 hours before bed, so its timing should not disturb your sleep. In a [[term:meta-analysis|meta-analysis]] of 23 studies, even evening exercise did not worsen sleep in healthy adults; it slightly increased slow-wave sleep (by 1.3 percentage points). Only vigorous exercise ending within about 1 hour of bedtime might lengthen sleep onset and shorten sleep [@Stutz2019_eveningExerciseMA]. Regular exercise improves sleep modestly: small benefits for total sleep time and efficiency, small to medium for the time taken to fall asleep, and moderate for subjective sleep quality [@Kredlow2015_exerciseSleepMA]. Your sleep quality may improve a little over the first 8-12 weeks of training (inference); your questionnaire scores will show whether it does.

- Train at about 13:00 (±1 hour) on training days; consistency matters more than the exact time.
- No hard sessions (intervals, heavy lifting) after about 02:00, that is within about 2 hours of bed. The evidence threshold is 1 hour; the extra hour is a buffer that also protects your dim-light period (practical convention).
- An easy walk after work, between about 01:00 and 02:00, is fine and adds steps; keep it conversational and avoid bright light (inference).
- Training after work (01:30-03:00) is not recommended: bright gym lighting in your biological evening conflicts with the light plan and shortens your wind-down (inference).

sections.title: Food and sleep
sections.body:
**Finish meal 4 by about 02:00.** In the [[plan:nutrition|nutrition plan]], your fourth meal comes after work at about 01:30-02:00. Finish it at least 2 hours before your 04:00 bedtime ([[dec:D20]]).

The evidence on meal timing and sleep is weak and observational. In 793 students, eating within 3 hours of bedtime was associated with more night awakenings (adjusted OR 1.43, 95% CI 1.00-2.04) but not with taking longer to fall asleep or sleeping less [@Chung2020_mealProximitySleep]. In US time-use diaries, eating or drinking within 1 hour of bed was linked with longer sleep but roughly two to 2.6 times the odds of prolonged night waking, and the associations weakened as the gap grew to 2-3 hours [@Iao2021_bedtimeEatingATUS]. Neither design can show cause.

**Make it protein-rich.** Meal 4 should carry at least about 0.4 g/kg of protein, which is about 30 g for you: curd or hung curd, paneer, eggs or milk. Dairy protein is mostly casein, which is digested slowly (standard nutrition science). Taking 20-40 g of casein about 30 minutes before sleep raises overnight protein synthesis [@Reis2020_presleepProteinSR], and a 12-week trial in young men found larger strength gains (summed [[term:1rm|1RM]] +164 vs +130 kg) and more quadriceps growth (+8.4 vs +4.8 cm²) with 27.5 g of pre-sleep protein each night than with a non-caloric placebo [@Snijders2015_presleep]. The protein group also ate more protein overall, so timing cannot be separated from amount; hitting your daily total of about 140-155 g matters more (inference).

**If you need a later snack.** If you are short of protein for the day, a small casein-rich serving (hung curd, paneer or milk) about 30 minutes before bed is reasonable. Avoid a large meal or a lot of fluid in the last hour, which risks night waking and bathroom trips (inference).

sections.title: Sleep inertia and the 13:00 session
sections.body:
[[term:sleep-inertia|Sleep inertia]] is the grogginess after waking. It impairs alertness and thinking, fades as you stay awake, and is worse after short sleep or when you wake at an adverse circadian time [@Hilditch2019_sleepInertiaReview]. After a full 8-hour sleep at the usual time, it decayed exponentially with time constants of 0.67 hours for subjective alertness and 1.17 hours for cognitive throughput, nearing baseline after 2-4 hours; getting up, showering, breakfast and ordinary room light (about 150 lux) did not abolish it [@Jewett1999_sleepInertiaTimeCourse]. From those constants, by 13:00 about three-quarters of the alertness deficit and a little over half of the cognitive deficit should be gone, and by 14:00 about 95% and 82% (our calculation). No study has measured lifting performance against time since waking, so the effect on your training is inference.

Your session also falls in your biological morning. In 10 trained men with conventional sleep times, bench-press and squat force were 2.6-3.3% and bar velocity 11.5-13.6% higher in the evening than in the morning, and an extended morning warm-up that raised body temperature to evening levels did not close the gap [@Pullinger2019_morning_warmup_lifts]. This matters little for results: strength gains and muscle growth were similar with morning and evening training, and strength adapted to the habitual training time [@Grgic2019_time_of_day_RT].

1. 12:00: get up on time, open the curtains and switch on bright lights.
2. 12:15: meal 1 ([[plan:nutrition]]); caffeine at about 12:30 if you use it.
3. 12:40-13:00: walk to the gym outdoors if practical, for daylight and as the start of your warm-up.
4. 13:00: do the full general warm-up from [[tool:warmup]] (8-12 minutes) rather than a shortened one ([[dec:D10]]), then the [[term:ramp-up-sets|ramp-up sets]] of your first exercise.
5. Do strength, flexibility and fitness tests at the same time after waking (about 1-1.5 hours) and after the same warm-up, so that results are comparable ([[plan:monitoring]]).

If your day allows, starting at about 14:00 (2 hours after waking) is an acceptable alternative but not required. If after 4-6 weeks your logs show that 13:00 sessions are consistently weaker than occasional later ones, consider the move.

sections.title: Tracking sleep
sections.body:
**Daily diary (one minute).** Fill it in soon after waking. The first seven items are core items of the Consensus Sleep Diary [@Carney2012_consensusSleepDiary]; the last three are specific to you.

| Item | Example |
|---|---|
| Time into bed | 04:05 |
| Time you tried to sleep | 04:15 |
| Time taken to fall asleep (estimate) | 20 min |
| Awakenings: number and total time | 2, 15 min |
| Final wake time | 11:50 |
| Time out of bed | 12:00 |
| Sleep quality (1-5) | 3 |
| Last caffeine: time and dose | 12:30, 100 mg |
| Meal 4 finished | 01:55 |
| Room dark: yes, partly or no | Partly |

Estimated sleep is the final wake time minus the time you tried to sleep, minus the time taken to fall asleep and the time awake during the night: 7 h 0 min in the example.

**Questionnaire every 4-8 weeks.** Complete the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) at baseline ([[phase:p0]]) and every 4-8 weeks; it asks about the past month. A global score above 5 separated poor from good sleepers with 89.6% sensitivity and 86.5% specificity [@Buysse1989_PSQI].

**Weekly review** (with [[tool:checkin]]): average estimated sleep, the number of nights under 7 hours, and any night when your bed or wake time moved more than 60 minutes from 04:00 or 12:00 (the 60-minute flag is pragmatic).

**Wearables.** Against laboratory polysomnography, several consumer devices, including a Fitbit model, matched or beat research actigraphy for telling sleep from wake, but all detected wakefulness poorly (specificity 0.18-0.54), so they tend to overestimate sleep. Their sleep-stage estimates were inconsistent, and accuracy fell on disrupted nights [@Chinoy2021_consumerSleepTrackers]. The models tested are not current ones, and none was tested on daytime sleep. If you buy a device ([[dec:D25]]), use it for bed and wake times and for duration trends, not for sleep stages or sleep scores, and cross-check it against your diary.

sections.title: When to seek help
sections.body:
**Insomnia.** See a doctor if, despite the bedroom, light and caffeine measures, you regularly take a long time to fall asleep or wake and cannot get back to sleep, and it affects how you function during your day. In this programme's terms: a PSQI above 5, or a month of diary entries showing that pattern (practical convention). Clinicians usually call insomnia chronic when it occurs on at least 3 nights a week for at least 3 months (diagnostic convention, not from the sources here).

The American College of Physicians recommends [[term:cbt-i|cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I)]] as the first treatment for all adults with chronic insomnia (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence); medication is considered only if CBT-I alone does not work, through shared decision-making [@Qaseem2016_ACPinsomniaGuideline]. CBT-I is a structured programme of sleep scheduling, stimulus control and work on unhelpful beliefs about sleep, delivered in person, by video or digitally. Your magnesium and L-theanine are reviewed in [[plan:supplements]]; they are not a substitute for it.

!> **See a doctor, and ask about a sleep study, if** you snore loudly most nights, someone sees you stop breathing or gasp in your sleep, you often wake with a headache, or you are sleepy during your day (for example dozing at your desk or while driving) despite 7-8 hours in bed. These suggest a different disorder, such as obstructive sleep apnoea, which needs different care (practical convention).

Also seek advice for an irresistible urge to move your legs at rest that keeps you awake, for acting out dreams, or for persistently low mood with changed sleep (practical convention; see [[plan:safety]] and [[sci:sci-behaviour]]).

pages.title: Daily activity
pages.tagline: More walking, shorter stretches of sitting, a five-minute mobility habit and sensible choices in the heat.
pages.summary: Your training sessions fill only a few hours a week; this page covers the rest of your day. Steps come first: measure your current daily average, then raise it by 1,000 steps a day every two weeks until you reach a floor of 7,000 and a target of 8,000-10,000. In large pooled studies most of the mortality benefit of walking is reached by about 8,000-10,000 steps a day in adults under 60, although your personal benefit is uncertain. Second, break up your nine-hour desk shift with 2-5 minutes of walking or standing every 30-60 minutes. Third, an optional five-minute daily mobility routine adds stretching frequency for your toe-touch goal, because range of motion improves with repetition and slips back when you stop. Fourth, you can swap an easy or steady aerobic session for a hike, a dance or martial-arts class, or a game of football or badminton, using the talk test to judge effort; keep the interval session in most weeks. Finally, heat: at 13:00, do cardio indoors and keep outdoor sessions for cooler times.

sections.title: Steps
sections.body:
**Targets.** A floor of 7,000 steps a day and a target of 8,000-10,000, judged as a 7-day average ([[dec:D24]]). 10,000 is optional, not a pass mark.

**Why these numbers.** Steps have a curved relationship with mortality: risk falls steeply from very low counts, then flattens. In a harmonised meta-analysis of 15 cohorts (47,471 adults), compared with the lowest quartile (median about 3,550 steps), quartiles with medians of 5,801, 7,842 and 10,901 steps had hazard ratios of 0.60, 0.55 and 0.47, with a plateau at about 8,000-10,000 steps in adults under 60 [@Paluch2022_stepsMortalityMA]. A 2025 meta-analysis of 57 studies found 7,000 versus 2,000 steps a day associated with 47% lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.46-0.60) and with lower risks of cardiovascular disease, dementia and depressive symptoms [@Ding2025_stepsHealthDoseResponse]. Another placed the flattening of the mortality curve at about 8,800 steps [@Stens2023_stepsDoseResponseMA], while a third found each extra 1,000 steps associated with 15% lower mortality and no clear upper limit up to about 11,500 [@Banach2023_stepsMortalityMA].

These are observational associations, mostly in older adults. In adults under 60, steps were not significantly associated with cardiovascular events over about 6 years, probably because there were few events [@Paluch2023_stepsCVDharmonisedMA], and twin data suggest that part of the activity-mortality link is genetic [@Karvinen2015_twinsGenesMortality]. Your personal health benefit is therefore uncertain. The practical reasons for you are that walking is the easiest way to raise your [[term:neat|non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT)]], which helps fat loss, and to offset long sitting (inference). More background is in [[sci:sci-aerobic]].

**Ramp.**

1. Measure: in [[phase:p0]], carry your phone in a trouser pocket during all waking hours for 7 days and note the 7-day average.
2. Add 1,000 steps a day to the weekly average every two weeks (practical convention for a gradual increase).
3. Stop increasing at 8,000-10,000. Once you have reached 7,000, do not let the weekly average fall below it.

| Starting average | Weeks 1-2 | Weeks 3-4 | Weeks 5-6 | Weeks 7-8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5,000 | 6,000 | 7,000 | 8,000 | 9,000 |
| 6,500 | 7,500 | 8,500 | 9,500 | Hold |
| 8,000 | 9,000 | 10,000 | Hold | Hold |

**Where the steps come from on your day.** Rough counts assume about 100 steps a minute when walking briskly (approximate; it depends on pace and stride).

| Time | Opportunity | Rough steps |
|---|---|---|
| 12:00-13:00 | Walk part of the way to the gym outdoors (also your daylight; [[plan:sleep]]) | 500-1,500 |
| About 15:15 | 10-15 minute walk after meal 2 | 1,000-1,500 |
| 16:00-01:00 | 2-5 minutes of walking every 30-60 minutes (next section) | 1,500-3,000 |
| About 19:30-20:00 | 10-15 minute walk in the meal break | 1,000-1,500 |
| Days off | A 30-60 minute walk, errands on foot or a hike | 3,000-6,000 |

**Energy.** Adding 3,000-4,000 steps a day (roughly 2-3 km) raises your expenditure by very roughly 100-150 kcal a day at 77 kg (rough arithmetic from the typical net energy cost of walking; inference). If your steps rise after you have calibrated your maintenance intake in Phase 0, expect your weight to drift down slightly at the same intake; the weekly check-in catches this ([[tool:checkin]], [[rule:energy-adjustment]]).

**How to measure.** A phone in your pocket is good enough for weekly averages, not for single walks. In a treadmill test at 5 km/h, a phone app counted total steps acceptably over longer walks, but for a 1,500-step walk its count differed from a wrist band's by between −573 and +377 steps [@Caputo2021_smartphoneSteps]. In laboratory tests, Fitbit, Apple Watch and Samsung devices counted steps accurately [@Fuller2020_wearablesSR]. The step-mortality studies mostly used hip-worn research accelerometers, and the associations were stronger with those than with wrist devices or pedometers [@Stens2023_stepsDoseResponseMA], so treat comparisons between your count and the targets as approximate. Steps taken without the phone (in the gym, around the house) are missed, so carry it consistently and keep the same device; then your trend stays valid. Tracking itself helps: programmes using consumer trackers increased daily steps more than similar programmes without them ([[term:smd|standardised mean difference (SMD)]] 0.24, 95% CI 0.16-0.33) [@Brickwood2019_trackersMA].

sections.title: Breaking up the desk shift
sections.body:
Your shift runs from 16:00 to 01:00. If you sit for most of it, you fall into the highest sitting category (more than 8 hours a day) of the largest analysis of sitting and mortality (inference from your schedule).

In that harmonised analysis of over one million adults, people who sat more than 8 hours a day and were in the least active quarter had 59% higher mortality (HR 1.59, 95% CI 1.52-1.66) than active people who sat less than 4 hours. People who sat as long but were in the most active quarter, roughly 60-75 minutes of moderate activity a day, had no clear excess risk (HR 1.04, 0.99-1.10) [@Ekelund2016_sittingActivityMortality]. The WHO advises limiting [[term:sedentary-time|sedentary time]] and replacing it with activity of any intensity, but the evidence did not allow a specific threshold [@Bull2020_WHOguidelines]. Structured training of 150-200 minutes a week averages only 20-30 minutes a day, so walking and short breaks have to supply the rest (inference).

**The rule.** Every 30-60 minutes, stand up and walk or stand for 2-5 minutes. No study has established the best interval; this one is a practical inference.

- Set a repeating 45-minute timer, or use a wearable's inactivity reminder.
- Refill a water bottle at the farthest cooler, which also keeps you hydrated.
- Take calls standing or walking.
- Use the stairs, and a toilet on another floor.
- Walk for 10-15 minutes after eating in the 19:30-20:00 break.
- If you work from home, walk a lap of the building or corridor, or do the mobility routine below.

Mechanistic reasoning, not tested for this pattern in the sources here: contracting muscle takes up glucose through a contraction-activated pathway that does not depend on insulin, which is one reason frequent breaks in sitting are thought to help metabolism.

sections.title: Optional 5-minute mobility routine
sections.body:
**Purpose.** To add stretching frequency for your toe-touch goal ([[dec:D27]]; tracked with [[ex:test-ftf]]) without adding gym time. Do it on any day you have not stretched your hamstrings after training, or simply every day: in a work break, after the shift or at home. The timing is not critical. It does not replace the warm-up before lifting ([[dec:D10]]).

| Order | Drill | Dose | Key points |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | [[ex:st-ham-bench]] or [[ex:st-ham-supine]] | 2 × 40 s per leg | Knee straight but not locked; hinge at the hips with a long spine; a strong but tolerable stretch, 6-7 out of 10 |
| 2 | [[ex:st-hip-flexor]] | 30 s per side | Squeeze the glute of the back leg and tuck the pelvis before leaning forward |
| 3 | [[ex:wu-open-book]] | 5 slow reps per side | Breathe out as you rotate; keep the knees stacked |
| 4 | [[ex:wu-ankle-rock]] | 10 rocks per side | Heel stays down; the knee travels over the middle toes |
| Optional | [[ex:bal-sls]] | 2 × 30 s per leg, left first | Your left leg balances worse ([[dec:D28]]) |

The hamstring stretch carries the toe-touch goal. The hip-flexor and thoracic drills are for comfort after long sitting, and the ankle rocks maintain the ankle bend you need for deep squats (practical convention; not tested in the sources here).

**Why frequency helps.** Regular stretching increases range of motion by about one standard deviation on average (effect size about 1.0, 95% CI 0.84-1.17) [@Konrad2024_chronic_stretch_ROM]. That meta-analysis found no clear effect of dose, but another synthesis linked larger gains to more weekly time and more frequent sessions and suggested stretching on at least 5 days a week [@Thomas2018_stretch_dose_ROM]. The extra range from a single session typically fades within about 30 minutes, so lasting change depends on repetition [@Behm2016_acute_stretching]. After 2-6 weeks without stretching, range of motion fell back part of the way, and people who had stretched more often each week kept more of it [@Konrad2025_detraining_ROM]. The ACSM minimum is about 60 seconds per muscle group on at least 2 days a week [@Garber2011_ACSM_position_stand]; this routine takes your hamstrings well past that.

**Mechanism.** In short programmes most of the gain is increased [[term:stretch-tolerance|stretch tolerance]]. After 3 weeks of hamstring stretching, muscle stiffness at a fixed angle was unchanged, but people tolerated a larger angle and more torque [@Magnusson1996_stretch_tolerance], and a meta-analysis of 3-8-week programmes found mainly sensory effects, with trivial changes in muscle and tendon properties [@Freitas2018_chronic_stretch_mechanics]. Tissue changes need longer or more intense stretching. Resistance training also improves range of motion, about as much as stretching, particularly in untrained people [@Alizadeh2023_RT_ROM]; the routine adds end-range exposure on top of your lifting (inference).

**Intensity and safety.** Stretch to 6-7 out of 10: in a 4-week trial, calf stretching at that intensity increased range by 40%, against 15% at 0-1 out of 10 [@Nakamura2021_HI_vs_LI_SS]. Stop if you feel sharp pain, numbness or tingling; nerve tissue can limit range independently of muscle [@Andrade2020_muscle_nerve_stretching]. More detail is in [[sci:sci-flexibility]].

sections.title: Activities that can replace a session
sections.body:
You can swap a scheduled easy or steady aerobic session ([[ex:cardio-steady]], [[ex:cardio-long]]) for an activity you enjoy. Keep the interval session ([[ex:cardio-int-4x4]]) as scheduled in most weeks, because it is your main stimulus for [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]] ([[dec:D13]]); which sessions are replaceable is inference. The overall aerobic plan is in [[dec:D11]].

| Activity | Can replace | What the evidence says |
|---|---|---|
| Hike, 2-4 hours (day off) | The long easy session | In outdoor walking groups (mostly uncontrolled studies), systolic blood pressure fell by 3.7 mmHg and VO₂max rose by 2.7 mL/kg/min, with good adherence [@Hanson2015_walkinggroups]; hills and rough ground make hiking at least as demanding (inference) |
| Dance class, 45-60 minutes | A steady session | Across 28 studies, dance improved body composition and musculoskeletal function more than other structured exercise, and cardiovascular function equally (low certainty; no pooled effect sizes reported) [@FongYan2018_danceMA] |
| Recreational football, about 60 minutes | A steady session; occasionally an interval session | In untrained men in their early 30s, 12 weeks of recreational football (3 × 60 minutes a week) raised relative VO₂max by 24.2%, against 21.5% for continuous running, and also improved jump height and sit-and-reach flexibility [@Milanovic2015_untrainedMenRunningRCT] |
| Martial-arts class (technique, pad work) | A steady session's time slot, not your VO₂max work | Combat-sport training improved standing long jump (effect size 1.04) and sit-and-reach (0.80) but not VO₂max (0.39, not significant) in students [@HernandezMartinez2025_combatsports]; adult studies report benefits for balance, but their designs are weak [@OriguaRios2018_martialarts] |
| Badminton, 45-60 minutes | A steady session | Not studied in this programme's evidence base; singles is more demanding than doubles (inference) |

**Judging equivalent effort.**

- Use the [[term:talk-test|talk test]]. Comfortable continuous speech usually means you are below the first [[term:ventilatory-threshold|ventilatory threshold]]; the point where speech first becomes difficult lies close to it [@Persinger2004_talkTest; @ReedPipe2014_talkTestReview]. A steady session is conversational: full sentences, but clearly harder breathing.
- Match the time. A class with instruction and pauses should last about 1.5 times the session it replaces, for example a 60-minute class for a 40-minute steady session (practical convention).
- Rate the whole session afterwards with the [[term:rpe|RPE]] scale in [[tool:intensity]]. For reference, on the 6-20 Borg scale the lactate threshold sat at about 11 and the individual anaerobic threshold at about 13-14, with an individual spread of about ±2 [@Scherr2013_RPE].
- Count a game as an interval session only if it included at least four bouts of 3-4 minutes in which you could say only a few words (inference).
- Log it in Hevy as a cardio entry with duration, session RPE and a 1-5 enjoyment rating ([[plan:logging]]).

**Fatigue and injury.** Football, dance and martial arts involve sprinting, jumping, turning and landing that your gym work does not yet prepare you for, so expect more [[term:doms|delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS)]] than usual after the first sessions (inference). Avoid them on the day before a hard lower-body session. Start martial arts with technique and pad work and leave full-contact sparring until the basics are secure (precaution; there are no injury data in this programme's evidence base). Increase a hike's duration or climb by no more than about 10% over your longest recent hike, by analogy with the running rule ([[rule:running]]; inference). Variety is worth having for its own sake, because enjoyment keeps you training ([[sci:sci-behaviour]], [[sci:sci-athletic]]).

sections.title: Heat
sections.body:
Your 13:00 slot falls close to the hottest part of the day in much of India for much of the year (general knowledge). Plan around it.

| Situation | Do this |
|---|---|
| Cardio at 13:00 | Indoors: treadmill, bike, rower or elliptical in an air-conditioned gym. For running in hot midday conditions, the treadmill is the sensible default (practical consideration) |
| Outdoor runs, hikes and long walks | Cooler times: the cooler months, late afternoon or evening on days off, or an easy walk after work around 01:00 where it is safe (no hard sessions after about 02:00; [[plan:sleep]]) |
| Walk to the gym in summer | Keep it short, use shade, wear a hat and carry water; a few minutes outdoors still gives far more light than indoors |
| First hot weeks of the year | Shorter, easier outdoor sessions at first (inference); see acclimatisation below |
| Humid or monsoon days | Humid heat adds to heat strain; slow down to stay at the same talk-test level, or move indoors (practical convention) |
| Very poor air quality | Move outdoor sessions indoors (practical convention; air pollution was not reviewed in this programme's evidence base) |

**Acclimatisation and fluids.** The first hot days of the year carry the most risk. Repeated exercise in the heat over 1-2 weeks is the most important single measure for reducing heat strain; start sessions well hydrated, limit dehydration during exercise, and schedule activity to minimise risk [@Racinais2015_heatConsensus]. Fluids are covered in [[plan:nutrition]].

!!> **Heat illness can be an emergency.** If you feel confused, unusually unsteady, faint or sick while exercising in the heat, stop at once, get into shade or air conditioning and tell someone. Exertional heat stroke is a medical emergency; survival depends on early recognition, stopping the activity and rapid whole-body cooling [@Roberts2021_ACSMheatIllness]. Warning signs and first aid are in [[plan:safety]].

pages.title: Monitoring and assessments
pages.tagline: What to measure, how to measure it, and which numbers to ignore
pages.summary: This page sets out what you measure during the programme, how to measure it so the numbers mean something, and how large a change must be before you believe it. The core is cheap and fully under your control: a daily morning weigh-in read as a 7-day average, a weekly navel waist measurement, full tape girths and progress photos every 4 weeks, your training log, and a short test battery at baseline and at the end of each phase. Your Renpho scale is excellent for weight and weak for everything else: its other 12 outputs are calculated from your weight, the height, age and sex you entered and, for most, one leg-to-leg impedance reading, and no independent validation of any Renpho scale was found. Tape-based body-fat equations are no more accurate for a single estimate, but they move only when your waist moves, which you can measure well. Every test has a measurement error; a change smaller than that error is noise, and early gains in strength and jump tests are partly skill learning. A wrist wearable is optional: useful for sleep timing, steps and resting heart rate, not for calories.

sections.title: What to measure and when
sections.body:
Measure a few things, the same way, at the same time of day. Fix the protocol (times, sites, devices, clothing) before [[phase:p1]] begins and keep it for the whole programme: most of what makes body measurements misleading is inconsistent conditions, not the instrument. When body composition was assessed without standardisation (no control of prior food, drink or activity), most methods blunted or exaggerated true change over 6 weeks [@Tinsley2021_trackingchange].

Four streams of data matter: your weight trend, your waist, your training log (load, reps and [[term:rpe|rating of perceived exertion (RPE)]] for every working set, in Hevy) and a periodic test battery.

| When | What | Time | How |
|---|---|---|---|
| Every day, on waking (about 12:00) | Body weight; read the 7-day mean, not the day | 1 min | Weigh-in protocol, next section |
| Every week, same weekday | Navel waist (two readings); this week's mean weight against last week's | 5 min | Tape protocol; [[tool:checkin]] |
| Every 4 weeks, same weekday | All 11 girth sites, progress photos, tape body-fat estimate | 25 min | [[ex:test-girths]]; [[tool:bodycomp]] |
| Every session | Load, reps and RPE for every working set | No extra time | [[plan:logging]]; [[tool:e1rm]] |
| Test week: at baseline, then the last week of each phase | The full test battery (section 7) | 2 gym sessions | [[dec:D03]] |
| Each test week, 3 mornings | Resting heart rate on waking; use the mean of the 3 | 2 min | [[ex:test-rhr]] |
| Optional, mid-phase | Push-ups, pull-ups, single-leg stance and fingertip-to-floor at the start of a session | 15 min | Same protocols as the test week |
| Whenever it happens | Confounders: creatine started, stopped or changed; illness; short sleep; travel; festivals; an unusually salty or large meal | 10 s | A dated note in your log |

**Reading the signals together**

No single number tells you whether the programme is working. Read the 4-week direction of three signals together. The interpretations below are inference, and the thresholds are judgement, set just above the measurement noise described in the sections that follow. [[term:recomposition|Body recomposition]] (losing fat while gaining muscle at a roughly stable weight) is the pattern Phase 1 aims for ([[dec:D04]]).

| 7-day mean weight, over 4 weeks | Navel waist, over 4 weeks | Training log | Most likely meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flat (within 0.5 kg) | Down 1 cm or more | Loads and reps rising | Recomposition: fat lost, muscle gained |
| Up 0.5-1 kg | Flat (within 0.5 cm) | Rising | Mostly lean gain |
| Up | Up 1 cm or more, sustained | Rising | Fat gain outpacing muscle gain: review intake |
| Down | Down | Holding or rising | Fat loss with muscle kept |
| Down | Flat | Falling | Too little food or recovery: check intake, sleep and illness before changing training |
| A sudden step | Unchanged | Unchanged | Water: creatine, salt, carbohydrate or a festival (check your notes) |

In a muscle-gain phase, a sustained rise in navel waist is the earliest practical sign that fat gain is outpacing muscle gain (inference). Intake changes go through [[rule:energy-adjustment]]; stalled lifts go through [[rule:stall]].

sections.title: Weigh-in protocol
sections.body:
Body weight is the one number your scale measures directly, and its trend is what calibrates your calorie targets. The day-to-day noise is larger than the weekly change you are looking for, so the protocol removes the avoidable noise and the 7-day mean removes most of the rest.

**Every morning**

1. Weigh straight after waking (about 12:00) and after emptying your bladder, before any food, drink, caffeine, supplements or training.
2. Same scale in the same spot, on a hard, level floor (tile or stone, not a rug or mat). If the scale has been moved, step on and off once to let it reset, then take the reading that counts (practical convention).
3. Same minimal clothing every time (underwear only), or none.
4. Stand still with your weight on both feet and take the first stable reading. Do not re-weigh for a better number.
5. Keep the raw value. Never edit or delete a reading because it looks wrong.

**How to read it**

- Use the 7-day rolling mean, and compare this week's mean with last week's. Act on a direction only when it holds for 2-4 weeks.
- Ignore single days. A kilogram gained overnight is water and gut content: as fat tissue it would need a surplus of roughly 7,700 kcal, an approximation that holds only for short-term, fat-dominated change [@Thomas2013_3500kcalRule].
- An exponentially weighted moving average works as well as a 7-day mean; no trial compares the two (inference).

**Why single days mislead**

- Weight cycles by about 0.3% across the week (heaviest Monday-Tuesday, lightest Friday), rises about 0.65% over a festive period such as Christmas-New Year and differs by up to about 0.5% between seasons [@Maher2023_weightfluctuation]. At 77 kg the weekly cycle alone is about 0.23 kg, as much as one to two weeks of weight change at the planned lean-gain rate of 0.1-0.25 kg/week (inference). A small observational study also found weight rising over weekends and falling on weekdays [@Orsama2014_weightRhythms], plausibly from weekend eating (inference); similar jumps around Indian festivals are plausible but unstudied.
- Glycogen is stored with about 3-4 g of water per gram, so a high- or low-carbohydrate day moves scale weight without any change in fat [@Kreitzman1992_glycogenWater].
- Salt, gut content and creatine-related water add noise that the sources reviewed did not quantify. Starting, stopping or reloading creatine can step your weight up or down through water (mechanism; size not quantified here), so log the date ([[plan:supplements]]).
- If daily errors were independent, a 7-day mean would shrink them by about √7, roughly 2.6-fold; they are partly correlated from day to day, so the real gain is smaller (statistical inference).

**Does daily weighing help or harm?**

Inside structured weight-loss programmes, adding self-weighing gave about 1.7 kg more weight loss ([[term:confidence-interval|95% confidence interval]] 0.8 to 2.6 kg); weighing alone, without a programme, showed no clear effect in the one trial available, and daily and weekly weighing instructions did not differ [@Madigan2015_selfweighingMA]. Across 29 tests, self-weighing was not associated with worse mood, body attitudes or disordered eating, although there was a small negative association with overall psychological functioning [@Benn2016_selfweighingpsych]. All of this comes from weight-loss trials and observational samples; none studied weighing during muscle gain. Your reason for weighing daily is statistical: daily points are what separate a slow trend from the weekly cycle.

!> If the daily number starts to drive your mood or your eating, weigh on three fixed mornings a week instead, or hide the daily value and look only at the weekly mean. The trend still works with fewer points; it just responds more slowly (inference).

**What the trend feeds**

Your provisional maintenance intake (about 2,700 kcal/day, plausible range 2,450-2,900) is an equation estimate. After 2-3 weeks of weighed-food logging and daily weigh-ins, your own data replace it: if the 14-day trend is flat (within about 0.1 kg/week), your average logged intake is your maintenance; otherwise each 0.1 kg/week of trend corresponds to about 110 kcal/day (0.1 kg × 7,700 kcal ÷ 7 days; a fat-tissue approximation, so less when part of the change is lean tissue or water). Self-reported intake is unreliable: in one small study, adults with obesity who believed they were diet-resistant under-reported their intake by about 47% [@Lichtman1992_underreporting], so the scale, not the food log, is the arbiter. [[tool:energy]] does the calculation and [[rule:energy-adjustment]] says when to change intake. Review every 2-4 weeks rather than weekly, because weekly adjustments chase water (practical convention; see [[plan:nutrition]]).

sections.title: Tape protocol
sections.body:
A tape measure is the cheapest instrument you own and, for the waist, the most informative. Its weakness is the operator, so the protocol fixes everything you can control. The technique below is standard expert practice; no source in this programme's evidence base quantified how reliable self-measured girths are, so the noise thresholds on this page are judgement (practical convention).

**Equipment**: a non-stretch fibreglass body tape, ideally with a spring-tension end or a self-retracting loop (it standardises tension); a full-length mirror; a skin marker for the first session.

**Rules for every site**

- Same state as the weigh-in: after waking and voiding, before food, drink and training. Never measure after a workout; trained muscles stay swollen for a while afterwards (inference).
- Stand upright and relaxed, feet hip-width apart, weight on both feet, muscles relaxed unless the site says flexed.
- Tape horizontal (check in the mirror), flat on the skin, not twisted, snug without dimpling the skin.
- Trunk sites (chest and both waists): read at the end of a normal, relaxed exhalation. Do not suck in or brace.
- Go round all sites once, then a second round. If the two readings at a site differ by more than 0.5 cm, take a third and record the median; otherwise record the mean to 0.1 cm (practical convention).
- Limbs: right side every 4 weeks; both sides at baseline and in each test week (practical convention).

Two sites feed equations: the navel waist and the neck give the [[term:navy-method|US Navy circumference method]] estimate, and the navel waist divided by your height gives your [[term:whtr|waist-to-height ratio]].

| Site | Landmark and position | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Neck | Just below the Adam's apple, tape sloping slightly down at the front; head level, eyes ahead | Feeds the Navy equation; do not tense the neck |
| Shoulders | Widest point around both shoulders, over the deltoids; arms relaxed at the sides | Hardest site to do alone; use the mirror or a helper |
| Chest | At nipple level, passing under the armpits; lower the arms once the tape is placed; end of a normal exhalation | |
| Waist, navel | Horizontal through the centre of the navel; abdomen relaxed; end of a normal exhalation | Primary waist site (now 86 cm) |
| Waist, narrowest | Narrowest point between the lowest rib and the top of the hip bone, seen from the front | Secondary site (now 81 cm) |
| Hips | Greatest backward bulge of the buttocks, feet together, glutes relaxed | |
| Arm, relaxed | Midway between the bony tip of the shoulder and the point of the elbow, arm hanging; mark the spot the first time | |
| Arm, flexed | Largest girth with the upper arm raised to shoulder height, elbow bent about 90°, biceps contracted hard | Least repeatable site; a loop tape helps |
| Upper thigh | Just below the fold of the buttock, weight on both feet | |
| Mid thigh | Halfway between the groin crease and the top of the kneecap | Measure the distance up from the kneecap once, note it, reuse it |
| Calf | Largest girth, weight on both feet; slide the tape up and down to find it | |

**Why the site matters.** Across 120 studies, the link between waist circumference and mortality, cardiovascular disease and diabetes was similar whether waist was taken at the minimal waist, midway between the lowest rib and the hip bone, or at the navel [@Ross2008_waistprotocol], and consensus guidance is to choose one protocol and keep it [@Ross2020_waistConsensus]. Absolute values do differ: yours are 86 cm at the navel and 81 cm at the narrowest point. Never mix sites in one series, and use the site that matches the equation it feeds.

**What your waist means now.** Your waist-to-height ratio is 0.48 at the navel (0.45 at the narrowest point), below the 0.5 boundary NICE uses for increased central adiposity [@NICE2025_NG246]. In a [[term:meta-analysis|meta-analysis]] of 31 studies with more than 300,000 adults, waist-to-height ratio discriminated hypertension, diabetes and cardiovascular risk slightly better than BMI or waist alone [@Ashwell2012_WHtR]. In north Indian men, proposed waist action levels were 78 cm (level 1) and 90 cm (level 2) [@Misra2006_IndianWaist]; you sit between them at both sites. For you the two boundaries coincide: a navel waist of about 90 cm is both the Indian level-2 point and a ratio of 0.5. An allometric analysis (in young people) argues that a fixed 0.5 may under-flag taller people [@Nevill2025_WHtRcritique], and at 181 cm you are tall for your population, so treat a navel waist trending towards 90 cm as the signal to act, not the point of arrival (inference). These are screening thresholds, not a diagnosis.

**Reading change (inference).** A 0.5 cm difference between two weekly waist readings is within tape noise; a 1 cm change that holds for 2-3 consecutive weeks is probably real. On the limbs, month-to-month changes under about 0.5 cm cannot be separated from noise, and arm and thigh girths change slowly even when training works ([[sci:sci-expectations]]).

sections.title: Progress photos
sections.body:
> No study was found that evaluated self-taken progress photos, judged by eye, as a measure of body-composition change or as an aid to adherence. Everything below is practical convention. Photos are a private qualitative record: never a number, and never the basis for a decision.

The nearest evidence is an algorithm applied to standardised smartphone photos, which estimated [[term:dxa|DXA]] body fat in men better than a foot-to-foot [[term:bia|bioelectrical impedance (BIA)]] scale: concordance 0.90 and root-mean-square error 2.9 percentage points, against 0.66 and 5.6 for the scale [@Nana2022_footBIAvsDXA]. The algorithm was developed by companies that employed several of the authors, and it is not the same as comparing pictures by eye. Photo-based body-fat apps also mean uploading near-nude images to a third party.

**Protocol (every 4 weeks, straight after the girths)**

1. Same place and plain background, same artificial light from above or in front. Close the curtains so that daylight, which changes with the season, does not move the shadows.
2. Phone on a shelf or tripod at navel height, about 2.5-3 m away, main (1×) lens; no wide-angle, zoom, filters or beauty mode. Mark the phone and foot positions on the floor with tape.
3. Same fitted shorts, no top. Same state: after waking, voiding and weighing, before food and training.
4. Use the self-timer, or record a short video and take still frames from it.
5. Four relaxed poses (not sucked in, not flexed), arms slightly away from the body: front, left side, back, right side. Add one flexed front pose if you want it.
6. Store them in a private, locked album with the date in the file name.

**How to compare.** Put the current set beside the set from 8-12 weeks earlier, pose for pose, at the same size. Do not compare with last month or with the mirror: over 4 weeks, differences in light and posture are usually larger than the change in your body (inference). Look at the outline (waist, shoulder-to-waist taper, arms, chest), not at abdominal definition on a given morning. If looking at the photos leaves you anxious rather than informed, look less often ([[sci:sci-behaviour]]).

sections.title: Your Renpho scale, critically
sections.body:
**The physics in one paragraph.** A foot-to-foot scale measures two things: weight, with load cells, and the [[term:impedance|impedance]] of a weak alternating current (50 kHz in single-frequency scales) that enters one sole, runs up that leg, crosses the pelvis and returns down the other leg [@Nunez1997_legtolegBIA]. Impedance combines resistance, from ionic body water, and reactance, from cell membranes acting as capacitors; at 50 kHz the current flows mainly through extracellular water [@Kyle2004_BIAprinciples; @Norman2012_phaseAngle]. A typical scale turns height²/resistance into total body water, turns water into [[term:ffm|fat-free mass (FFM)]] by assuming FFM is about 73% water [@Wang1999_hydrationConstant], and calls the rest of your weight fat: fat itself is never measured. Leg-to-leg impedance alone predicted FFM and body water less well than arm-to-leg BIA, and caught up only when age, sex and waist-to-hip ratio were added as covariates [@Nunez1997_legtolegBIA]; BIA equations hold only in the population they were built in, and only at normal hydration [@Kyle2004_BIAprinciples]. Your arms and most of your trunk lie outside the current path, and anything that moves water (a meal, a drink, sweat, glycogen, creatine) moves the fat number (mechanism; shown directly for meals and fluid with bioimpedance spectroscopy in athletes [@Kerr2017_foodfluid]). The outputs are therefore largely functions of the height, age and sex you typed in plus your weight, with one leg impedance reading as an extra input (inference: Renpho's equations are unpublished).

**The 13 outputs**

| Output | Measured or derived | Verdict | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Weight | Measured (load cells) | **Use** | A direct measurement and your primary daily number |
| BMI | Derived: weight ÷ height² | Ignore | Exact arithmetic that adds nothing to weight, and it rises as you gain muscle. Your 23.5 is just above the Asian action point of 23 [@WHO2004_AsianBMI], which says little about a lifter |
| Body fat % | Derived: weight minus predicted FFM | Use with caution | Individual error of several percentage points, error for change about 2 points even in the better devices, and it moves with water |
| Fat-free body weight | Derived: impedance plus entered height, age and sex | Use with caution | The mirror image of body fat %; limits of agreement about ±5 kg in male athletes [@Nickerson2019_FFBIAmen] |
| Muscle mass | Derived from the same FFM estimate | Ignore | No information beyond FFM, and it includes water |
| Skeletal muscle | Derived: a further equation on the same reading | Ignore | A leg current cannot separate skeletal muscle from other lean tissue |
| Body water | Derived: the quantity closest to the physics | Ignore | Computed from the same reading, so it moves in mirror image to body fat % and cannot check it; it swings with food and fluid |
| Protein | Derived | Ignore | Impedance cannot sense protein; a fixed share of FFM (inference) |
| Bone mass | Derived | Ignore | The current does not resolve bone; set mainly by entered height and weight (inference) |
| BMR | Derived: an equation on weight, height, age, sex or predicted FFM | Ignore | Not measured. Published equations give you about 1,634-1,906 kcal/day depending on the equation and the fat-free mass estimate (Mifflin-St Jeor: 1,751); maintenance calibrated from your weight trend is better ([[tool:energy]]) |
| Subcutaneous fat | Derived | Ignore | Not sensed; a share of the body fat estimate (inference) |
| Visceral fat | Derived index | Ignore | The current path does not cross your abdomen, so trunk fat is not sensed (inference from the physics); use the navel waist instead |
| Metabolic age | Derived: predicted BMR compared with age norms (inference; method unpublished) | Ignore | A comparison with no physiological definition |

**What the validation evidence says**

No peer-reviewed validation of any Renpho scale, including your Elis 1, was found in PubMed, so its error is unknown. Its nearest relatives give the picture:

- Repeatability is excellent: precision error for repeated readings was 0-0.5 percentage points across 15 consumer and research devices. Accuracy for an individual is not: against a 4-compartment model, the standard error of estimate (SEE) was 3.1-7.5 points and average bias ranged from −3.5 to +11.7 points depending on the device; for change over 12-16 weeks the SEE was still 1.7-2.6 points across devices [@Siedler2022_15BIAdevices].
- A Tanita foot-to-foot scale against DXA in men: root-mean-square error 5.6 points, concordance 0.66 [@Nana2022_footBIAvsDXA]. Foot-to-foot BIA against a 3-compartment model in male college athletes: limits of agreement ±5.7 points and ±5.2 kg FFM, with proportional bias, so leaner and fatter users are misestimated in consistent directions [@Nickerson2019_FFBIAmen].
- Unstandardised conditions (recent food, drink or exercise) blunted or exaggerated true change [@Tinsley2021_trackingchange], and meals and fluid alone shifted impedance-based fat and FFM estimates substantially [@Kerr2017_foodfluid].
- Renpho's equations are unpublished, and BIA equations built in Western samples may not transfer to South Asian men (inference).

The trap is high repeatability with poor accuracy: the number is stable enough to look trustworthy. The body-fat change you can realistically make in a few months is about the size of the error for change, so the scale cannot resolve it (inference). The decision record is [[dec:D23]]; the background is in [[sci:sci-bodycomp]].

**If you want to use body fat % at all**

1. Same conditions every day: the weigh-in state, with bare, clean, dry feet centred on the electrodes.
2. Never read a single day. Use the weekly mean, and compare means at least 8-12 weeks apart.
3. Treat changes smaller than about 3 percentage points as noise, and look for about 5 before you are confident (inference: roughly twice the error for change).
4. Expect steps when creatine, illness or a festival shifts your water; check your notes before believing a change.
5. Never let it overrule the waist and weight trends.

+> A positive control, if your app allows a second user profile: set one up with your height and sex but an age 15 years older, step on under each profile on the same morning, and compare. Whatever differs in body fat, muscle or metabolic age came from the typed-in numbers, not from your body (inference). Delete the test profile afterwards.

sections.title: Body-fat estimates from the tape
sections.body:
A tape equation is no more accurate than the scale for a single estimate, but it has one decisive advantage: it moves only when your waist (or neck) moves, and you can measure those well. Use one method consistently and let [[tool:bodycomp]] do the arithmetic. Three equations are in play: the US Navy method, [[term:rfm|relative fat mass (RFM)]] and the BMI-based Deurenberg equation.

| Method | Inputs | Your estimate | Validation and error |
|---|---|---|---|
| US Navy | Navel waist minus neck, and height | 16.7% (waist 86 cm, neck 38 cm) | Waist minus neck ranked fatness better than BMI or waist alone against DXA [@Friedl1997_circumferenceDXA]; in 1,904 soldiers, circumference equations underestimated DXA by about 4.4-5.9 points in men [@McClung2025_CBEvsDXA] |
| RFM | 64 − 20 × height ÷ waist | 21.9% (navel) or 19.3% (narrowest) | Beat BMI against DXA in large US national survey samples [@Woolcott2018_RFM]; no systematic bias against DXA in 61 young Mexican adults, R² 0.84 [@GuzmanLeon2019_RFMvalidation]; derived with waist measured at the top of the hip bone |
| Deurenberg | 1.20 × BMI + 0.23 × age − 10.8 × sex (men = 1) − 5.4 | 19.1% | SEE 4.1 points, and it overestimates in obesity [@Deurenberg1991_BMIequation]; because it uses BMI, it counts gained muscle as gained fat |

**The honest answer is a range.** Any one of these carries an individual error of about ±4-6 percentage points, and none has been validated in South Asian men in the sources reviewed. Allowing for the Navy method's known underestimate, together they put you at about 20% body fat (plausible range 17-24%). Your FFM is then about 61.6 kg (58.5-63.9) and your [[term:ffmi|fat-free mass index (FFMI)]] about 18.8 kg/m² (17.9-19.5), close to the median of 18.9 kg/m² in Swiss men aged 18-34 [@Schutz2002_FFMIpercentiles]; in one preliminary study, drug-free male athletes rarely exceeded a height-adjusted FFMI of 25 [@Kouri1995_FFMI]. [[sci:sci-expectations]] explains what that means for your ceiling.

**Which one to track (judgement): RFM on the navel waist.**

- It needs only the measurement you already take every week.
- It has no neck term. With the Navy equation, a neck 1 cm larger at the same waist lowers the estimate by about 0.8 points (arithmetic), so neck and trapezius growth from training would read as fat loss.
- It showed no systematic bias against DXA in its external validation.
- RFM was derived with waist at the top of the hip bone; of your two sites, the navel is usually nearer that level (inference).

Keep the Navy value as a monthly cross-check, and drop Deurenberg once training has added muscle. Whichever you choose, never switch mid-series.

**Sensitivity.** At your size, each 1 cm of navel waist moves RFM by about 0.5 points and the Navy estimate by about 0.8 points (arithmetic). The tape body-fat trend is therefore your waist trend in different units: it gives you a scale you can relate to, not new information. A 0.5 cm tape error is worth about 0.25 points of RFM.

**What the tape cannot tell you** is whether the weight you gain is muscle. A stable waist with rising weight and rising loads is the best available proxy for lean gain (inference), which is why the three signals in the first section are read together.

**DXA.** One scan at baseline and one at the end of each phase would anchor these estimates. DXA has its own error but was more robust than BIA to lapses in standardisation [@Tinsley2021_trackingchange]. Its cost and availability where you live were not assessed; it is optional.

sections.title: The test battery
sections.body:
The battery runs at baseline and in the last week of each phase, and covers resting heart rate, [[term:vo2max|VO₂max]], strength, power, balance and flexibility ([[dec:D03]] explains the choice). Each drill page has the full protocol and scoring; this section covers the order, the error of each test and how to read a change.

**How big must a change be?** Reliability is usually reported as an intraclass correlation (ICC; 1.0 means identical results on retest). The minimal detectable change (MDC) is the smallest change that exceeds measurement error with 95% confidence (MDC95 = 1.96 × √2 × the standard error of measurement). A change smaller than the MDC may be real, but you cannot know it. Early gains in rep and jump tests are partly skill and [[term:neural-adaptation|neural adaptation]], so they overstate change in muscle.

**Test week (practical convention)**

| Day | On waking | At the gym (about 13:00) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Resting heart rate, weigh-in, girths and photos | Standard warm-up, then single-leg stance, fingertip-to-floor, knee-to-wall, broad jump, push-ups, pull-ups and the optional plank; 3-5 min between maximal tests |
| 2 | Resting heart rate | Rest, or light upper-body training only |
| 3 | Resting heart rate | Aerobic test: the Rockport walk, or the 2.4 km run once you have moved to it |

Keep the order, warm-up, time of day, footwear and surface identical every test week. Do not stretch before the flexibility tests. In one small study (16 adults) of extreme morning and evening types, whole-body flexibility rose about 2.4 cm after a 30-minute rather than a 5-minute warm-up and varied by about 3 cm between 08:00 and 20:00 [@Edwards2026_diurnal_flexibility]: the same order as the changes you are tracking (inference). Postpone the week if you are ill or have slept badly ([[rule:illness]]).

| Test | Measures | Your baseline | Real change | Read it as |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [[ex:test-rhr]] | Resting heart rate: a slow marker of aerobic fitness and autonomic tone | Not yet recorded | No MDC sourced; use the 3-morning mean | A gradual fall over months fits rising fitness |
| [[ex:test-rockport]] | VO₂max estimated from a 1.6 km walk | Baseline test | Cross-validated SEE 0.355 L/min, about 4.6 mL/kg/min at 77 kg [@Kline1987_Rockport]; individual 95% band about ±9 mL/kg/min (2 × SEE) | Direction matters more than level |
| [[ex:test-run-2400]] | VO₂max estimated from a 2.4 km run | Not until you can run about 20 min continuously | Highest validity of the distance tests, r 0.79 (0.73-0.85) [@MayorgaVega2016_walkrunMA] | The first attempt is partly a pacing lesson |
| [[ex:test-pushup]] | Upper-body strength-endurance | 5 reps | About 2 reps (15-s timed version) [@Negrete2010_UEtestsMDC] | +3 reps or more on the same standard is likely real |
| [[ex:test-pullup]] | Pulling strength relative to body weight | 3 reps | About 2 reps (modified pull-up) [@Negrete2010_UEtestsMDC]; between-day ICC 0.87-0.98 across a soldiers' test battery that included pull-ups [@Lester2014_pullupReliability] | +3 reps or more is likely real; extra body weight makes it harder |
| [[ex:test-plank]] | Trunk endurance (optional) | 60 s | No reliability data in the sources reviewed | Only large changes, such as 60 to 90 s, count (inference) |
| [[ex:test-broad-jump]] | Lower-body power | Baseline after two familiarisation sessions | 29 cm on first exposure; about 1 cm after familiarisation [@MarinJimenez2024_SLJ] | Count only post-familiarisation results |
| [[ex:test-sls]] | Static balance, each leg | Eyes open: left 20 s, right 30 s. Eyes closed: left 10 s, right 15 s | Best-of-3 inter-rater ICC 0.994-0.998 [@Springer2007_unipedalstance]; no MDC sourced | Eyes-open times rising towards the 45-s cap, and the left-right gap closing |
| [[ex:test-ftf]] | Whole-chain forward bend | Fingertips above the floor | No MDC for healthy adults; treat under 3 cm as noise (inference) | Distance above the floor shrinking |
| [[ex:test-knee-wall]] | Ankle dorsiflexion, each side | Baseline test | 1.6-1.9 cm [@Powden2015_WBLT_reliability] | More than 2 cm is real |
| [[ex:test-girths]] | Size and shape | Waist 86 cm (navel), 81 cm (narrowest) | Self-measurement reliability unknown | See the tape protocol |

**Resting heart rate.** Count for 60 s on waking, after a few quiet minutes in the same position each time (lying or seated: pick one), before caffeine; or use a wearable's resting value. Caffeine, short sleep, heat, illness, dehydration and alcohol all raise it, so one reading means little. In a meta-analysis of 87 prospective studies (48 for this outcome), each 10 bpm higher resting heart rate was associated with 17% higher all-cause mortality (RR 1.17, 1.14-1.19), but the data are observational and heterogeneous, so it is a marker rather than a proven lever [@Aune2017_RHRmeta]. Use it as a slow trend, not a daily go/no-go rule; an unusually high or irregular reading, especially with symptoms, warrants medical review ([[plan:safety]]).

**Rockport walk.** You walk 1.6 km as fast as you can on a flat, measured course and record the time and your heart rate at the finish; the drill has the equation, which was derived in adults aged 30-69 [@Kline1987_Rockport]. With the other inputs held constant, each 10 bpm lower finishing heart rate raises the estimate by 0.115 L/min (about 1.5 mL/kg/min at 77 kg), and each minute faster raises it by 0.224 L/min (about 2.9 mL/kg/min) (arithmetic from the published equation). The heart-rate reading is the weak link: a chest strap is best, because wrist sensors err more during movement than at rest [@Bent2020_PPGinaccuracy]. Heat and humidity raise heart rate and so lower the estimate; keep the time, place and conditions the same (inference).

**From walk to run.** The 2.4 km run is a maximal effort that depends on pacing. Stop this or any test at once for chest pain or pressure, faintness, unusual breathlessness or palpitations, and follow [[plan:safety]]. Switch to it only once you can run about 20 minutes continuously (judgement), and do both tests in that first test week so the two series overlap ([[rule:running]], [[dec:D14]]). [[sci:sci-aerobic]] covers what VO₂max is and how it responds to training.

**Push-ups and pull-ups.** Fix the standard on the drill page (depth, lockout, no kipping) and never change it; a rep that misses the standard does not count. In 1,104 male firefighters, those doing more than 40 push-ups had far fewer cardiovascular events over 10 years than those doing fewer than 10 (incidence rate ratio 0.04, 0.01-0.36) [@Yang2019_pushups]; with 37 events and no adjustment for aerobic fitness, that is a prognostic association, not a target. Your 5 sits in that cohort's lowest group. No civilian adult pull-up norms were found.

**Plank (optional).** Forearm plank, elbows under the shoulders, body in one straight line from head to heels; stop at the first loss of that line (hips sagging or piking), not at discomfort, and record the seconds. No reliability data were found, so only large changes count (practical convention).

**Broad jump.** On first exposure the retest was about 12 cm longer from learning alone (ICC 0.94, CV 7.1%), and the MDC fell from 29 cm to about 1 cm after familiarisation [@MarinJimenez2024_SLJ]. Do two familiarisation sessions in the weeks before the baseline counts (practical convention; the study did not report how long its learning period was). In 410 adults the jump reflected lower-body explosive strength (R 0.78 against laboratory power and force measures, with sex, fat and lean mass in the model) [@MarinJimenez2024_SLJ].

**Single-leg stance.** Barefoot, same surface, left leg first, best of 3 per leg and condition, using the reference protocol: arms crossed on the chest, raised foot near but not touching the standing ankle, eyes on a wall target, 45 s maximum. Under that protocol, men aged 18-39 reached a best-of-3 of 44.4 s (SD 4.1) with eyes open, so nearly everyone hits the cap, and 16.9 s (SD 13.9) with eyes closed, with no sex difference [@Springer2007_unipedalstance]. If your baseline was taken the same way, both your eyes-open times (left 20 s, right 30 s) sit below about 36 s, roughly 2 SD under the mean and a crude marker of a genuine deficit because of the ceiling, while your eyes-closed times (10 and 15 s) are within the normal spread (inference). The reference sample stood on one leg of their choice, so it gives no norm for a left-right gap; yours is a trackable asymmetry, not a diagnosis, and closing it is the aim of the balance work ([[dec:D28]]).

**Flexibility.** Fingertip-to-floor had an ICC of 0.99 and correlated very strongly with radiographic trunk flexion (r −0.96) in back-pain patients [@Perret2001_fingertip_floor_test]; it measures the whole chain (hamstrings, hips, spine and nerves), not hamstring length alone. Record the middle-fingertip-to-floor distance, positive above the floor, best of 3. Knee-to-wall, each side: foot pointing straight at the wall, heel down, slide the foot back until the knee only just touches the wall, and record the largest toe-to-wall distance. Its MDC of 1.6-1.9 cm comes from clinician measurement; the reliability of measuring it on yourself is unknown [@Powden2015_WBLT_reliability]. See [[dec:D27]].

sections.title: Wearables
sections.body:
A wearable is optional; nothing in the programme depends on one. What it is good for depends on the sensor.

**What a wrist device can and cannot measure**

| Quantity | Wrist optical device | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Steps | Accurate in laboratory studies (Fitbit, Apple, Samsung) | [@Fuller2020_wearablesSR] |
| Resting heart rate | Reasonably accurate | [@Bent2020_PPGinaccuracy] |
| Heart rate in steady cardio | Moderate: error about 30% larger than at rest, and Fitbit models tended to read low | [@Bent2020_PPGinaccuracy; @Fuller2020_wearablesSR] |
| Heart rate on arm-driven machines or while lifting | Poor: all optical devices were poor on an elliptical with arm levers; lifting was not tested, but gripping and wrist flexion are the worst case for the sensor (inference) | [@Gillinov2017_HRmonitors; @Bent2020_PPGinaccuracy] |
| Calories burned | Inaccurate for every brand | [@Fuller2020_wearablesSR] |
| Total sleep time and wake after sleep onset | No significant difference from polysomnography (sleep-staging Fitbits) | [@Haghayegh2019_FitbitSleep] |
| Sleep stages and time to fall asleep | Rough: wake specificity 0.58-0.69, and time to fall asleep underestimated | [@Haghayegh2019_FitbitSleep] |
| VO₂max estimates, readiness or stress scores, blood oxygen | Not evaluated in the sources reviewed | None |

The sensor explains the pattern. A wrist device shines light into the skin and infers the pulse from changes in light absorption by pulsing blood (photoplethysmography); movement corrupts the signal, and the sensor can lock onto your step cadence instead of your pulse. Skin tone was not a significant source of error [@Bent2020_PPGinaccuracy].

**Chest strap for intervals.** A chest strap senses the heart's electrical signal directly: a Polar H7 agreed almost perfectly with ECG (concordance 0.996), while wrist devices ranged from 0.67 to 0.92 [@Gillinov2017_HRmonitors]. Where heart rate feeds a decision (the finishing heart rate of the Rockport walk, the work bouts of 4 × 4 intervals in [[dec:D13]]), use a Bluetooth chest strap paired with your phone or a watch. You do not need one to start: Phase 1 cardio is designed to work without a heart-rate monitor ([[dec:D11]]). Device presets assume an age-predicted [[term:hrmax|maximum heart rate (HRmax)]]; yours is about 186 bpm by the Tanaka equation, with an individual error of about ±20 bpm, so preset zones may be off by a zone or more for you (inference). [[tool:intensity]] sets zones you can check against effort.

**Phone step counting** costs nothing, but the only phone study in this evidence base was of very low quality (limits of agreement −573 to +377 steps against a wrist band over a 1,500-step walk) [@Caputo2021_smartphoneSteps], and a phone lying on your desk through a 9-hour shift counts nothing (inference).

**The Fitbit question**

*What it is.* According to Google's help pages, the Google Fitbit Air is a screenless band with a status light. It tracks steps, sleep (with stages shown in the app) and heart rate, estimates blood oxygen during sleep (not in all regions), can flag an irregular rhythm that may indicate atrial fibrillation, syncs by Bluetooth to the Google Health app, and puts advanced features behind a Google Health Premium subscription (3 months included) [@GoogleHelp2026_FitbitAir]. The specification page, seen only through a search summary, lists optical heart rate, a 3-axis accelerometer and gyroscope, red and infrared blood-oxygen sensors, a temperature sensor and GPS through your phone [@GoogleHelp2026_FitbitAir]. No independent validation of the Air was found, and results for older Fitbits may not transfer to it.

*Is it worth buying for you?* The value of each use, judged against the evidence above ([[term:smd|SMD]] is a standardised mean difference; 0.2 is conventionally a small effect):

| Use | Value for you | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Sleep timing and duration | Moderate | Useful on an unusual 04:00-12:00 schedule ([[plan:sleep]], [[dec:D22]]); total sleep time is the most valid sleep output [@Haghayegh2019_FitbitSleep] |
| Resting heart rate trend | Moderate | Replaces manual counts; optical sensing is reasonably accurate at rest [@Bent2020_PPGinaccuracy] |
| Steps | Moderate | Accurate counts [@Fuller2020_wearablesSR]; tracker-based interventions raised daily steps more than interventions without them, SMD 0.24 (0.16-0.33) [@Brickwood2019_trackersMA]; useful against a long desk shift ([[plan:activity]]) |
| Heart rate in intervals and tests | Low | No screen to read live, and optical error rises with movement |
| Calories for setting food intake | None | Inaccurate for every brand [@Fuller2020_wearablesSR]; your weight trend sets intake |
| Heart rate while lifting | None | Gripping and wrist flexion are expected to defeat the sensor (inference) |

*Verdict (inference).* Optional and low priority. Buy it if you want an effortless record of sleep, steps and resting heart rate; it may also nudge your daily steps up a little. Skip it if money is tight: the weight trend, the tape and the training log do the essential monitoring. If you want one device for training rather than lifestyle, buy a chest strap instead. If you do wear the band, wear it on top of the wrist as Google advises [@GoogleHelp2026_FitbitAir], ignore its calorie figure and treat its sleep stages as rough. The reasoning is recorded in [[dec:D25]].

pages.title: Safety and stop rules
pages.tagline: Screen once, build up gently, know the few signs that mean stop, and make solo lifting fail-safe.
pages.summary: You are a healthy 31-year-old with no symptoms, so current guidance does not require a doctor's clearance before you start: a two-minute PAR-Q+ self-check is enough, and any YES answer sends you to a doctor first. The real risks for someone in your position are few and specific: doing far too much too soon in the first weeks, which can cause exertional rhabdomyolysis (a dangerous breakdown of muscle); heat illness if you exercise outdoors around 13:00 in a hot climate; and being trapped or struck by a free weight when training alone. This page sets out what the programme does to prevent each of these, the short list of symptoms that mean stop at once and get help, how to set safety arms and bail out of a failed lift, how to breathe on heavy sets, how to tell normal soreness from injury with a 0-10 pain scale, when illness means no training and how to come back, and the warning signs that an aesthetic goal is turning into an unhealthy preoccupation. Save the emergency numbers in your phone before your first session.

sections.title: Before you start: screening
sections.body:
**Plain version.** If you are healthy, have no symptoms and have no diagnosed heart, metabolic or kidney disease, you do not need a doctor’s clearance to start. Complete the PAR-Q+ self-check (the official form is at eparmedx.com) once before your first session. NO to all seven questions: start. YES to any: stop here and see a doctor or a qualified exercise professional first.

**Why that is enough.** The American College of Sports Medicine dropped its old practice of counting risk factors, which generated excessive physician referrals that could deter people from exercising. Its screen now rests on three factors: how active you currently are, whether you have symptoms or known cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease, and how hard you intend to exercise [@Riebe2015_ACSMscreening].
