The PAR-Q+ turns that logic into a self-check: NO to all seven page-1 questions clears you for unrestricted activity, and any YES leads to follow-up questions, where a further YES leads to the ePARmed-X+ or a qualified exercise professional [@PARQplusCollab2025_PARQplus]. In a cohort of 1,670 adults screened this way, with extra screening for anyone above 160/90 mmHg, all were cleared for maximal exercise and no adverse events occurred, although a cohort of this size cannot rule out rare events [@Yee2019_PARQplusBPcutpoints]. The full reasoning for your case is in [[dec:D02]].

**What it implies for you.** At 31, healthy and on no medication, you will very probably clear the screen. But you have never trained, and the same three-factor logic points to starting at light-to-moderate effort and building up (inference from the ACSM model). That is why the first two weeks of [[phase:p1]] stop sets 3-4 [[term:rir|reps in reserve (RIR)]] short of failure and keep cardio conversational.

| Situation | What to do |
|---|---|
| NO to all seven PAR-Q+ questions | Start; note the date |
| Any YES, for example chest pain, dizziness or loss of consciousness, or a diagnosed chronic condition | Do not start yet; complete the PAR-Q+ follow-up pages or see a doctor [@PARQplusCollab2025_PARQplus] |
| Resting blood pressure at or above about 160/94 mmHg | See a doctor before hard training; the Yee cohort authors proposed below 160/94 mmHg as the cut-point for clearing people to maximal exercise [@Yee2019_PARQplusBPcutpoints] |
| A close relative died suddenly of a heart problem at a young age | Discuss with a doctor before vigorous training (inference) |
| A new symptom, diagnosis or medication at any later point | Repeat the PAR-Q+ before the next session |

**Two cheap extras (inference; neither tool requires them).** Have your resting blood pressure measured once at a pharmacy or clinic, and record your resting heart rate ([[ex:test-rhr]]) with the baseline tests ([[dec:D03]]). Repeat the PAR-Q+ every 12 months; that validity period is quoted in secondary sources and was not verified from the official form.

sections.title: Stop immediately and get help
sections.body:
!!> Stop at once and get emergency help if, during or soon after exercise, you have any sign in the first four rows below. Do not finish the set, try to ‘walk it off’ or drive yourself to hospital.

| Sign | What it can mean | Action (practical convention) |
|---|---|---|
| Chest pain, pressure, squeezing or fullness lasting several minutes or coming and going; discomfort in the jaw, neck, back, one or both arms or shoulders [@CDC2024_heartAttackSymptoms] | Heart attack or reduced blood flow to the heart | Stop, sit or lie down, call emergency services, tell gym staff |
| Unusual shortness of breath, especially with or before chest discomfort [@CDC2024_heartAttackSymptoms] | Heart or lung problem | Stop; call emergency services if it does not settle within a few minutes of rest or comes with any other sign here |
| Fainting or near-fainting; sudden weakness, light-headedness or a cold sweat [@CDC2024_heartAttackSymptoms] | Heart-rhythm or blood-pressure problem | Lie down with legs raised; call emergency services after any faint during exercise |
| Confusion, odd behaviour, slurred speech, staggering or collapse, especially in heat | Exertional heat stroke (see the heat section) | Call emergency services and start cooling at once [@Roberts2021_ACSMheatIllness] |
| Palpitations: a racing, pounding or irregular heartbeat that does not settle within a few minutes of rest (practical convention) | Heart-rhythm disturbance | Stop for the day; same-day medical assessment; emergency services if it comes with chest pain, breathlessness or faintness |
| A sudden, severe headache during a lift, especially with vomiting, neck stiffness or changed vision (inference; not covered by the sources reviewed) | Bleeding or another blood-vessel problem | Stop and seek emergency care |

**Why a short, specific list.** Vigorous exertion, particularly by unfit people, can briefly raise the risk of sudden cardiac death and heart attack in susceptible individuals, even though regular activity and fitness lower coronary risk overall [@Franklin2020_AHAexerciseRisk]. Such events are often preceded by warning symptoms, and the risk falls as people become more active [@Riebe2015_ACSMscreening]. For a healthy 31-year-old the absolute risk is very low (inference; the sources read give no absolute rates), so the useful levers are a gradual build-up of intensity and acting on symptoms immediately. ‘Listen to your body’ is too vague for someone who cannot yet tell normal training discomfort from danger (inference).

**Heart rate is not the stop signal.** Your estimated maximum heart rate ([[term:hrmax|HRmax]]) is about 186 bpm, but the individual error on that estimate is about ±20 bpm, so a number on a watch cannot tell you when you are in danger; symptoms can (inference).

**Before your first session (practical convention):**
- Save the emergency numbers in your phone. In India, 112 is the national emergency number and 108 is the ambulance number in most states; check which works where you live.
- Ask the front desk whether the gym has an automated external defibrillator (AED) and where it is kept.
- Keep your phone within reach during the session, not in a locker, and tell someone your usual training time (about 13:00).
- After any red-flag episode, do not train again until a doctor has assessed you, then repeat the PAR-Q+.

sections.title: Exertional rhabdomyolysis: the beginner’s overdose risk
sections.body:
**Plain version.** [[term:rhabdomyolysis|Exertional rhabdomyolysis]] is a rare but serious condition in which a burst of unaccustomed, excessive exercise breaks down so much muscle that its contents flood the blood and can injure the kidneys. It is the main reason your first sessions feel easier than they could be.

**Mechanism.** Damaged fibres leak creatine kinase (CK) and myoglobin into the blood; myoglobin passes into the urine, darkens it and can cause kidney insufficiency, which is the main danger [@Backer2022_exertionalRhabdoSR; @Rawson2017_exertionalRhabdo]. The intracellular cascade (membrane damage, calcium overload, protease activation, myoglobin-induced tubular injury) will be familiar to you; it is background physiology, not something the sources here tested.

**Who gets it.** In a pooled series of 772 athletes, patients were mostly young men (mean age 28.7 years), 14.8% of cases followed weightlifting, and CK at presentation averaged about 31,500 IU/L, ranging from 164 to over 106,000 [@Backer2022_exertionalRhabdoSR]. Listed causes and co-factors include unaccustomed exercise, exercise that is improperly prescribed or used as punishment, temperature extremes, infections, drugs and inherited disorders; creatine monohydrate does not appear to be a trigger, so your creatine needs no change [@Rawson2017_exertionalRhabdo]. Case series cannot give a risk per session.

| Risk factor | Applies to you? | What the programme does |
|---|---|---|
| Unaccustomed exercise | Yes: you have never trained | Weeks 1-2 at 3-4 RIR with modest sets per new exercise; volume builds gradually ([[dec:D06]], [[dec:D07]]) |
| High-volume [[term:eccentric|eccentric]] (lowering) work: many slow negatives, high-rep ‘finishers’, long downhill walks or runs | Only if you add extras | No finishers, circuits or extra negatives in the first month; [[ex:pull-up]] negatives only as prescribed |
| Many sets to [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]] | Possible | No failure in weeks 1-2; later, failure only on machines and isolation exercises. Failure also brings more fatigue and worse in-session feelings than stopping 1-3 reps short [@Refalo2023_proximityFatigue; @Refalo2025_proximityPerceptual] |
| Heat and dehydration | Yes, if you train outdoors around 13:00 | See the heat section |
| Infection | Occasionally | [[rule:illness]]: no hard training while ill |
| Exercise as punishment for a missed session or a large meal | Never here | Missed sessions are rescheduled, never doubled up |

The pattern to avoid, in one sentence: a first or comeback session with many hard sets, heavy lowering emphasis and little rest, in the heat (inference from the case-series features above). The same caution applies after any long break; see [[rule:breaks]].

**Normal soreness is different.** [[term:doms|Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS)]] is a diffuse ache and stiffness of a whole muscle, starting hours after unaccustomed exercise and usually gone within a week [@MuellerWohlfahrt2013_Munich_consensus]. Expect it after your first sessions and after each new exercise; it shrinks quickly as the [[term:repeated-bout-effect|repeated-bout effect]] develops, a protection that was still present 6 months after a single eccentric bout [@Nosaka2001_RBE_duration].

!!> **Same-day medical assessment (emergency department)** if, typically 24-72 h after a session, you have muscle pain or swelling far beyond what the session should cause, a limb that is markedly weak or tight and swollen, or dark, tea- or cola-coloured urine. Say that you recently did unaccustomed strenuous exercise; a blood CK test confirms or excludes it. Do not train again until cleared. (Presenting features from the case series; the time window and actions are practical convention.)

sections.title: Heat: training at 13:00 in a hot climate
sections.body:
**Plain version.** In an air-conditioned gym, heat is a minor issue. It matters for anything outdoors around midday (runs, run-walks, long walks, hikes), in a gym without cooling during the hot season, and on the first hot days of the year before you are used to them.

**Evidence.** Exertional heat stroke is a medical emergency with a risk of organ injury and death; survival depends on early recognition, stopping activity and rapid whole-body cooling, and outcome probably relates to how long severe hyperthermia lasts. Most exertional heat illness can be prevented by recognising and modifying its risk factors [@Roberts2021_ACSMheatIllness]. Heat acclimatisation is the single most important preventive measure, built through repeated exercise-heat exposures over 1-2 weeks; sessions should start well hydrated, dehydration during exercise should be limited, and activity should be scheduled to minimise heat exposure, especially on the first hot days of the year [@Racinais2015_heatConsensus].

**Mechanism.** Most of the energy working muscle uses appears as heat; when sweat evaporation and skin blood flow cannot shed it, core temperature climbs (background physiology). Acclimatisation expands plasma volume, brings on earlier and heavier sweating and lowers heart rate and core temperature at a given workload (background physiology; not verified in the abstracts read).

**Your rules (the consensus applied to your schedule; inference):**
- On day one, find out whether the gym is air-conditioned. If it is not, in hot months keep cardio conversational and shorter, and use a fan.
- In hot weather, do outdoor sessions such as [[ex:cardio-runwalk]] and [[ex:cardio-long]] in the cooler part of your day, or move them onto a treadmill or bike. Your 13:00 slot falls in the hot part of a typical Indian day (general knowledge).
- When you begin exercising outdoors in heat, keep the first 1-2 weeks short and easy and lengthen sessions as you acclimatise.
- Start hydrated: drink with your first meal after waking and take a bottle of about 0.5-1 L to every session; for long or very sweaty sessions use an electrolyte drink (practical convention).
- Pale-straw urine before training is a rough sign of adequate hydration (practical convention).
- Shorten or skip outdoor sessions on extreme days, when ill and after a short night; illness and sleep loss reduce heat tolerance (general consensus; not quantified in the sources read).

**Recognising heat illness.** The consensus distinguishes heat exhaustion from heat stroke [@Roberts2021_ACSMheatIllness]; the symptom lists below are standard first-aid teaching (practical convention).

| Stage | Typical signs | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Heat cramps or heat exhaustion | Heavy sweating, fatigue, headache, dizziness, nausea, cramps; thinking still clear | Stop; move to shade or air-conditioning; lie down with legs raised; sip water or an electrolyte drink; no more exercise that day |
| Heat stroke (emergency) | Confusion, odd behaviour, slurred speech, staggering, collapse or seizure; hot skin, with or without sweating | Call emergency services; cool immediately, ideally by immersing the body in cold water, otherwise by continuous dousing with cold water plus fanning and ice packs; keep cooling until help arrives |

!> Confusion during exercise in the heat is heat stroke until proved otherwise. If you see it in someone else, cool first and keep cooling while help is on the way (practical convention, consistent with the consensus emphasis on rapid cooling).

sections.title: Training alone: make every lift fail-safe
sections.body:
**Plain version.** Lifting is one of the safer ways to exercise, but when you train alone the main acute hazard is being trapped under, or struck by, a free weight. The fixes are mechanical and take seconds.

**Evidence.** Injury rates in bodybuilding-style training are low, about 0.24-1 injury per 1,000 hours, mostly strains, tendinitis and sprains of the shoulder, lower back, knee, elbow and wrist [@Keogh2017_weightTrainingInjury]. Emergency-department records show where the serious acute injuries come from: in 65.5% a weight dropped on the person, 90.4% involved free weights, and free-weight injuries were more often fractures or dislocations than machine injuries (23.6% vs 9.7%; injury proportion ratio 2.44, 95% CI 1.92-3.09) [@Kerr2010_weightTrainingED]. Those records include home lifters and have no exposure denominators, and no trial has tested the countermeasures below; they follow from the mechanism (inference). On the other side of the ledger, strength training itself cut sports injuries by about two-thirds in randomised sports injury-prevention trials, an indirect population (risk ratio 0.315, 95% CI 0.207-0.480) [@Lauersen2014_injury_prevention].

**Equipment rules**
1. **Barbell squat and bench press only in a power rack or Smith machine with [[term:safety-arms|safety arms]] or pins** ([[ex:back-squat]], [[ex:bb-bench-press]], [[dec:D15]]). Squat: arms about 2-5 cm below the bar at the bottom of your deepest rep. Bench: arms a little below the point where the bar touches your chest, so that if you fail you can flatten your back and let the bar settle on them. Test the height with an empty bar (practical convention).
2. **Collars on every loaded barbell, every time.** Plates sliding off one end tip the bar.
3. **No barbell lift to failure.** Keep 2-3 RIR on free-weight [[term:compound-exercise|compound exercises]]; true failure is reserved for machines and [[term:isolation-exercise|isolation exercises]], where you can simply let go ([[dec:D07]]). [[dec:D08]] starts you on machines and dumbbells partly for this reason.
4. **Clear floor.** Plates racked, dumbbells back on the rack, nothing behind you where you step back or lower dumbbells.
5. **Phone within reach**, and someone who knows when you train.

**How to bail out.** Practise each with an empty bar or light dumbbells before you need it (practical convention).

| Lift | If you cannot finish the rep |
|---|---|
| Barbell squat in a rack | Keep hold of the bar and sit straight down until it rests on the safety arms, then slide out from under it. Without safety arms, do not back-squat alone. |
| Barbell bench press in a rack | Lower the bar to your chest under control, flatten your back so it settles on the arms, then slide out towards the head end. |
| Dumbbell bench or incline press ([[ex:db-bench-press]], [[ex:incline-db-press]]) | Lower the dumbbells to your chest, then down to the floor at your sides with elbows bent, or bring them to your thighs and rock up to sitting. Never let go of them over your face. |
| Seated dumbbell shoulder press ([[ex:db-shoulder-press]]) | Lower to your shoulders, then to your thighs. |
| Machines | Return the stack under control; keep fingers clear of the stack and moving parts; set any range-of-motion stops before the set. |
| Pull-up, assisted pull-up and dip | Step down on to the platform or a box; do not drop from the top position. |

**Learning technique without a coach.** Use outcome-directed cues on compound lifts (‘push the floor away’, ‘drive the bar straight up’): across many experiments, an external focus improved performance (g = 0.26) and retained learning (g = 0.58) compared with attending to body parts [@Chua2021_externalFocusMA]. Film one working set of each new lift from the side, and also from the front for squats, and compare it with the exercise page. In a small randomised trial, reviewing video of one’s own squats after each set improved technique, and the gains were retained for up to a week [@Shin2023_videoFeedbackSquat]; a physiotherapist chose what to correct in that trial, so self-review is a reasonable but untested substitute. One or two sessions with a qualified coach to review your videos would be good value if affordable (inference).

sections.title: Breathing, bracing and blood pressure
sections.body:
**Plain version.** On most sets, breathe out as you push or pull and in as you lower. On the hardest reps of heavy compound lifts, take a breath at the top, hold it briefly while you brace your trunk, and breathe out as you pass the hardest point. Avoid long, grinding reps with a sustained breath-hold.

**Mechanism.** Three things add up to raise blood pressure in heavy lifting: contracting muscle squeezes its own vessels, a reflex pressor response raises arterial pressure, and a [[term:valsalva|Valsalva manoeuvre]] (straining against a closed glottis) raises pressure inside the chest, which is transmitted to the arteries. Pressure rises in each [[term:concentric|concentric]] phase and climbs as failure approaches [@MacDougall1985_BPheavyLifting].

**Evidence.** With direct intra-arterial measurement in five experienced bodybuilders, a double-leg press to failure produced a mean peak of 320/250 mmHg, one person exceeding 480/350; even a single-arm curl to failure reached 255/190 mmHg [@MacDougall1985_BPheavyLifting]. These are brief peaks, and the American Heart Association judges resistance training safe and effective for adults with and without cardiovascular disease [@Paluch2023_AHAresistanceTraining]. No trial has compared breathing instructions on health outcomes, so the middle path below is inference (low confidence).

| Situation | Breathing |
|---|---|
| Warm-up sets, machines, isolation work, any set above about 10 reps | Continuous: out on the effort, in on the lowering |
| Last 1-3 reps of heavy compound sets (squat, leg press, Romanian deadlift, presses), once technique is stable | Breathe in at the top, [[term:bracing|brace]] the trunk, hold through the hardest part of the rep (a second or two), breathe out as you pass it |
| A rep slowing into a long grind | Do not hold your breath through it; end the set |
| Sudden severe headache mid-set | Stop; see the stop-signs table |

Stopping most sets 1-3 reps short of failure also avoids the largest peaks, because pressure climbs as failure approaches [@MacDougall1985_BPheavyLifting]. If a blood-pressure reading comes back high, or you are ever diagnosed with an eye, blood-vessel or heart condition, get individual medical advice about heavy lifting (general clinical caution, not sourced here).

sections.title: Pain rules: soreness, niggles and injury
sections.body:
**Plain version.** Some discomfort is part of training; what matters is its kind, its size and its trend. For any pain in a joint, a tendon or one specific spot, use a 0-10 scale (0 = none, 10 = worst imaginable) and follow [[rule:pain]].

| Kind | Typical features | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Effort burn | During the set, in the working muscle, gone within a minute or two | Normal; nothing to log |
| DOMS | Diffuse ache and stiffness of a whole muscle or group, starting hours after a session (often new or lowering-heavy work), sometimes mild swelling, fading within about a week [@MuellerWohlfahrt2013_Munich_consensus] | Train as planned, easing the load on that muscle if needed. Soreness is not proof that a session worked: in rats it developed without detectable muscle damage [@Mizumura2024_DOMS_neurochemistry] |
| Possible injury | Sudden sharp or stabbing pain at a precise moment in a set, a well-localised tender spot, bruising or a palpable gap [@MuellerWohlfahrt2013_Munich_consensus]; or joint pain that keeps coming back | Stop that exercise today; rate the pain; apply the thresholds below |

**The [[term:pain-monitoring|pain-monitoring]] approach.** Instead of stopping everything at the first twinge, or training through anything, you keep training with modification while pain stays mild, settles by the next morning and is not trending upward week to week. In a [[term:rct|randomised controlled trial]] in Achilles tendinopathy, continuing running and jumping under a pain-monitoring model improved function as much as six weeks of rest (VISA-A-S score 57 to 85 versus 57 to 91 at 12 months, no significant difference), with no harm detected [@Silbernagel2007_painMonitoringRCT]. At five years 80% had fully recovered, and greater fear of movement went with poorer recovery of heel-rise endurance (r = −0.59) [@Silbernagel2010_achilles5yr]. In a tiny pilot trial (15 people), pain-guided activity gave better treatment compliance than pain-free restriction (86% vs 67%) [@Sprague2021_painGuidedActivity]. These were patients with tendon problems, so the transfer to a healthy beginner is indirect.

**Thresholds used in this programme** (practical convention; the numeric limits of the original model were not verified for this programme):

| Pain in a joint, tendon or one spot | Action |
|---|---|
| 0-3/10 during the exercise, back to normal by the next morning, not worse than last week | Acceptable: continue as planned |
| 4-5/10 during the exercise, or still present the next morning | Modify next time: lighter load, shorter [[term:rom|range of motion]], slower lowering, or a variant that does not hurt ([[rule:substitution]]); hold progression on that exercise until it settles |
| Above 5/10, sharp, or changing how you move | Stop that exercise today and use a pain-free alternative |

**See a physiotherapist or doctor within days** for sharp or joint-line pain, pain that changes how you move or makes you limp, swelling, numbness, tingling or weakness, pain not settled after about 7 days, or pain that keeps worsening over 1-2 weeks despite modification (care thresholds are inference from the sources above plus general clinical practice). Running pain follows the site-by-site version in [[rule:running]]. Same-day care is for the red flags in the sections above.

Write the rating in the Hevy note for that exercise, for example ‘L knee 2/10, gone next morning’, so the trend is visible over weeks.

sections.title: Illness: when not to train and how to come back
sections.body:
**Plain version.** Mild cold symptoms above the neck and no fever: an easy session is optional. Fever, body aches, chest symptoms, or vomiting and diarrhoea: no training. Come back over three sessions. The exact steps are in [[rule:illness]].

**Evidence status.** No source in this programme’s evidence base tests training during or after common infections, so the ‘neck check’ below is consensus practice in sports medicine, not tested outcome evidence. Sourced facts that support caution: infections are among the listed causes of exertional rhabdomyolysis [@Rawson2017_exertionalRhabdo]; most exertional heat illness is preventable by modifying risk factors [@Roberts2021_ACSMheatIllness], and illness is commonly listed among them (general consensus; not stated in the abstract read). The classic reason for ‘no training with a fever’ is that viral infections occasionally inflame the heart muscle (myocarditis), when hard exercise is considered dangerous (background clinical knowledge, not sourced here).

| Symptoms | Training |
|---|---|
| Above the neck only (runny or blocked nose, sneezing, mild sore throat) and normal temperature | Optional easy session: about half the planned sets at RIR 3-4, conversational cardio, no intervals; stop if you feel worse |
| Fever (38 °C or above, or feeling feverish), chills, body aches, chest congestion or a chesty cough, shortness of breath | No training until 24-48 h without fever, without fever-reducing medicine |
| Vomiting or diarrhoea | No training until you have eaten and drunk normally for 24 h; dehydration adds heat and kidney risk |
| Chest pain, palpitations, fainting or unusual breathlessness during or after an illness | No training; see a doctor first |

**Coming back (practical convention):**
1. First session: about 50-60% of the planned sets at RIR 3, easy cardio only, indoors.
2. Second session: about 75% of the sets at RIR 2-3.
3. Third session: back to the plan, if the first two felt normal.
4. After more than about 2 weeks off, use [[rule:breaks]] and [[tool:breaks]] instead.

Mark missed sessions as skipped in this app and do not double up to catch up. A few days off do not undo your progress (inference; [[term:detraining|detraining]] is covered in [[sci:sci-progression]]).

sections.title: Mental health and body image
sections.body:
**What to expect.** Exercise tends to help mood. An umbrella review of 97 meta-analysed reviews (1,039 trials) found moderate reductions in depressive symptoms (median effect size −0.43), anxiety (−0.42) and psychological distress (−0.60), with healthy adults among the groups benefiting most and larger effects at higher intensity [@Singh2023_PAmentalHealthUmbrella]. Most underlying reviews were of low quality, so treat this as a likely bonus, not a treatment. If low mood lasts more than a couple of weeks, see a professional (practical convention).

**Body image can go either way.** On average, exercise improves body image only slightly [@Campbell2009_exerciseBodyImageMA], and not in every group studied [@CasusoHolgado2024_exerciseBodyImageBreastCancer]. With aesthetics as your first goal, the risk worth knowing about is muscle dysmorphia: an obsessive preoccupation with not being muscular enough, plus compulsive behaviours such as excessive training, rigid dieting and frequent body checking. Its severity correlates with obsessive-compulsive traits, and anabolic-steroid users score higher (d ≈ 0.45) [@Cinaroglu2025_muscleDysmorphiaMA]. Body-image concern correlates with exercise-addiction risk (r = 0.26) [@Guo2025_bodyImageExerciseAddiction], and heavy social-media use is associated with symptoms in early data [@VintroAlcaraz2025_socialMediaMD]. The muscle-dysmorphia evidence is all cross-sectional or qualitative, so the causal direction is unknown.

**Safeguards built in (inference; no validated in-app screener exists):**
- Photos and tape measurements on a fixed schedule ([[ex:test-girths]]), not daily; body-composition numbers treated as noisy trends ([[dec:D23]]).
- Expectations set from data rather than from social media ([[dec:D26]], [[sci:sci-expectations]]).
- Every 4-8 weeks, answer six questions honestly:

1. Do I worry most days that I am not muscular enough, despite visible progress?
2. Do I feel guilty or distressed when I miss a session?
3. Have I trained through an injury or illness this month?
4. Is my eating so rigid that I avoid meals with other people?
5. Do I check mirrors or take body photos many times a day?
6. Am I considering anabolic steroids or other performance drugs?

If several answers are yes, or one is a strong yes, talk to a mental-health professional. In India, the national Tele-MANAS line (14416) is free; check that it is current. Adherence, habits and wellbeing are covered in [[sci:sci-behaviour]], and the safety science behind this page in [[sci:sci-safety]].

pages.title: Using this programme with your workout app
pages.tagline: Set Hevy up once, log three numbers per set, review once a week.
pages.summary: This programme says what to do; Hevy records what you actually did; a short weekly review turns that record into next week’s targets. Set-up takes about half an hour: one Hevy routine per session template, named exactly as in this app (for example ‘P1 · Full body A’), each exercise added under the ‘Log as’ name shown on its page, with rest timers and supersets copied from the session page. In every working set you record three numbers: weight, reps and RPE, which here is simply 10 minus your reps in reserve. Warm-up sets are marked as warm-ups, and short notes capture pain, technique and machine settings. After each session you tick it done in this app. Once a week you enter your check-in, run the progression calculator on any stalled lift and plan the next week; monthly and at the end of each phase you repeat measurements and tests. Export your data from both apps regularly. Logging is worth the minute it takes: self-monitoring is one of the best-supported techniques for sticking with exercise.

sections.title: Set up once
sections.body:
Allow about 30 minutes before your first session, and repeat this at every phase change.

1. **One routine per session template.** In Hevy, make a routine folder for each phase (‘Phase 1’) and inside it one routine per session template in this app, named identically: ‘P1 · Full body A’, ‘P1 · Full body B’ and so on. Matching names let you pair a Hevy workout with its session page at a glance.
2. **Add exercises by their logging names.** Each exercise page shows ‘Log as: …’ with the exact Hevy name to search for. One name per movement keeps one continuous history, which is what the progression and [[term:e1rm|estimated 1RM (e1RM)]] calculators ([[tool:progression]], [[tool:e1rm]]) work from. Never log one movement under two names, or two variants (say, dumbbell and machine press) under one.
3. **Missing from Hevy’s library?** Create a custom exercise with exactly the ‘Log as’ name, its equipment type and its primary muscle.
4. **Put the prescription in the exercise note** so it is on screen mid-session: sets, rep range and the [[term:rir|reps-in-reserve (RIR)]] target, for example ‘3 × 8-12 @ RIR 2 · seat 5’. Machine settings go here once you have found them.
5. **Rest timers.** Set each exercise’s rest timer to the value given on the session page.
6. **Supersets.** Where the session page pairs exercises as a [[term:superset|superset]], link them with Hevy’s superset option so they alternate and the timer runs after the pair.
7. **Left side first.** Start every [[term:unilateral|unilateral exercise]], such as [[ex:split-squat]], [[ex:sl-rdl]] or [[ex:step-up]], with the left side, the leg that balances worse ([[dec:D28]]), and match the right side’s reps to the left (practical convention). Add ‘L first’ to the note.
8. **Cardio.** Add the cardio sessions ([[ex:cardio-steady]], [[ex:cardio-runwalk]], [[ex:cardio-int-intro]]) as time-and-distance exercises so they sit in the same history.

+> Hevy’s menus change between versions. If a step looks different, keep the principle: one routine per template, one name per exercise, targets visible during the set.

sections.title: What to record in every set
sections.body:
| Field | What to enter | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Weight | Kilograms on the bar or stack, or of one dumbbell; on assisted pull-up or dip machines, the assistance (less is harder) | Progression is calculated from it |
| Reps | Full-range reps completed; partial reps go in the note | [[term:double-progression|Double progression]] needs honest reps |
| RPE | 10 − RIR, on every working set (conversion table at the end of this page) | Effort targets and calibration |
| Set type | Warm-up sets marked as warm-up; deliberate sets to failure marked as failure | Keeps warm-ups out of your working-set history |
| Note | Pain (site and 0-10), technique, machine settings, ‘filmed’ | Pain trends, repeatable set-up, technique review |

+> Hevy shows what you did last time beside each set. That is the number to beat, by a rep or, once the rep range is complete, by load ([[rule:double-progression]]).

**Rate effort straight after the last rep.** The programme prescribes effort as RIR, which Hevy records as [[term:rpe|RPE]]. Expect early estimates to be off: on average people under-predicted the reps they had left by about one (0.95, 95% CI 0.17-1.73), with very large differences between people and studies (I² 97.9%), and predictions were more accurate close to failure and in sets of 12 reps or fewer [@Halperin2022_RIR_accuracy]. Training experience did not clearly change accuracy [@Remmert2023_RIRtrainedUntrained].

**Calibrate in Phase 1 weeks 5 and 9, then every 4-6 weeks** ([[rule:rir-calibration]]). On one safe machine or isolation exercise (leg extension, machine row, cable curl), note the RIR you would call at your target rep, then keep going to true [[term:momentary-failure|momentary failure]] and log the extra reps in the note (‘called RIR 2, got 4 more’). If you are consistently out by 2 or more, adjust how hard you push working sets. This routine is practical convention built on the accuracy findings above; it has not itself been tested. Never do it on barbell lifts ([[plan:safety]]).

**Warm-up sets.** Mark the [[term:ramp-up-sets|ramp-up sets]] from [[tool:warmup]] as warm-up sets and leave their RPE blank.

**Notes worth writing:**
- ‘L knee 2/10 during, gone next morning’ (for [[rule:pain]])
- ‘Seat 4, back pad 2, handles middle’ (machine settings)
- ‘Last 2 reps hips rose early; filmed’ (technique)
- ‘Flat today: slept 5 h’ (context for a poor session)

**Cardio.** Log duration, distance where available, a session RPE (0-10) and, for runs, any pain 0-10 at the knee, shin, foot or ankle, and hip, which [[rule:running]] uses.

sections.title: After each session
sections.body:
1. **Finish the workout in Hevy** and check that every working set has weight, reps and RPE.
2. **Tick the session done in this app.** The tick feeds the weekly view and your adherence count. If you skipped or shortened the session, record that rather than leaving it blank.
3. **Copy the plain-text session if useful.** The session page can be copied as plain text; paste it into the Hevy workout’s description or your own notes to keep plan and record side by side.
4. **Next-morning check** (30 seconds after waking). Is any pain from yesterday still there? Add the 0-10 rating to that exercise’s note. Plain muscle soreness needs no logging, though a quick ‘quads sore 4/10’ helps you spot patterns after new exercises.

**Why it is worth the minute.** In a meta-regression of healthy-eating and physical-activity interventions, self-monitoring explained more of the variation in success than any other technique, and interventions that paired it with at least one other self-regulation technique (such as goals, feedback or review) were more effective (effect size 0.42 vs 0.26) [@Michie2009_BCTmetaRegression]. The weekly review below is that second technique.

sections.title: Once a week: review and plan
sections.body:
Pick a fixed slot, for example the day after your last session of the week, and give it 10-15 minutes.

| Step | Where | What you decide |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Check-in | [[tool:checkin]] | Enter the week’s weigh-ins and waist measurement (protocols on [[plan:monitoring]]) |
| 2. Progress | Hevy history and [[rule:double-progression]] | Which exercises earned more load or reps next week |
| 3. Stalled lifts | [[tool:progression]] and [[rule:stall]] | For any lift the stall rule flags, run the calculator and apply its suggestion |
| 4. Effort check | Hevy notes and [[rule:rir-calibration]] | In calibration weeks, whether your called RIR matches what the failure sets showed |
| 5. Pain and illness | Hevy notes, [[rule:pain]], [[rule:illness]] | Which exercises are modified or on hold, and when they return |
| 6. Energy | [[tool:energy]] and [[rule:energy-adjustment]] | Whether food intake changes, as the rule specifies |
| 7. Plan | This app | Next week’s sessions and times; a missed session moves to the next free day rather than being doubled up |

**Adherence check (inference).** If you miss more than about one session in four over a month, simplify the plan rather than pushing harder, and rewrite your if-then plan, for example ‘when I finish my first meal after waking, I leave for the gym’. If-then plans of this kind increased physical activity modestly in trials that reinforced them (effect 0.25, 95% CI 0.05-0.45) [@Silva2018_implementationIntentionsMA].

sections.title: Monthly and at the end of each phase
sections.body:
| When | What | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Monthly | Tape measurements (girths) and progress photos, same conditions each time | [[ex:test-girths]], [[tool:bodycomp]] |
| Monthly | Two-minute checks: toe-touch and single-leg stance (ankle test optional) | [[ex:test-ftf]], [[ex:test-sls]], [[ex:test-knee-wall]] |
| Every 4-8 weeks | The six body-image questions | [[plan:safety]] |
| End of each phase | Repeat the baseline battery: walk or run test, push-ups, pull-ups, broad jump, single-leg stance (left and right, eyes open and closed), toe-touch, ankle test, resting heart rate | [[ex:test-rockport]] or [[ex:test-run-2400]], [[ex:test-pushup]], [[ex:test-pullup]], [[ex:test-broad-jump]], [[ex:test-sls]], [[ex:test-ftf]], [[ex:test-knee-wall]], [[ex:test-rhr]] |
| End of each phase | Transition checklist: what changes in training, food and targets, and new Hevy routines for the next phase | [[tool:transition]] |
| End of each phase | Export both apps | See Backups below |

The [[plan:monitoring]] page holds the protocols and takes precedence if its schedule differs. Add a one-line Hevy note on test days so the training log shows when testing happened. Your starting points for comparison: 5 push-ups, 3 pull-ups, a 60 s plank, and single-leg stance of 20 s on the left versus 30 s on the right with eyes open, 10 s versus 15 s with eyes closed.

sections.title: Backups
sections.body:
Your records live in two places, and either can be lost with a phone, a reinstall or a cleared browser.

- **This app:** Settings → Export saves your records here as a file. Keep the file somewhere other than this device, such as cloud storage or an email to yourself.
- **Hevy:** its settings include an export of your workout data (a CSV file). Hevy also keeps your history in your account, but a separate copy protects you if you lose access.
- **When:** at the end of every month and every phase, and before changing phone or browser.
- **Naming:** put the date first (‘2026-11-30 programme export’) so the latest copy is obvious.

sections.title: Reading RPE in Hevy
sections.body:
Hevy’s RPE field follows the reps-in-reserve version of the RPE scale, so the conversion is simple: **RPE = 10 − RIR**.

| Hevy RPE | Reps in reserve | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 0 | No further rep possible with good form (momentary failure) |
| 9.5 | 0 | No further rep, but slightly more load might have been possible |
| 9 | 1 | One more rep possible |
| 8.5 | 1-2 | One more for sure, maybe two |
| 8 | 2 | Two more possible |
| 7.5 | 2-3 | Two more for sure, maybe three |
| 7 | 3 | Three more possible |
| 6 or lower | 4 or more | Moderate effort |

So a target of RIR 2 means logging RPE 8, RIR 1-2 means RPE 8-9, and the 3-4 RIR of your first fortnight means RPE 6-7. If Hevy does not show an RPE column, switch on RPE tracking in its workout settings. Leave RPE blank on warm-up sets.

**Why effort-based loading rather than percentages.** In a trial matched for sets and reps, loads chosen by RPE gave strength and muscle-thickness gains similar to loads set as percentages of [[term:1rm|one-repetition maximum (1RM)]] (squat 1RM +17.1 kg with RPE vs +13.9 kg with percentages; difference not significant) [@Helms2018_RPEvsPercent], and a meta-analysis found no significant difference in 1RM gains between autoregulated loading (RIR-based RPE or bar velocity) and fixed percentages [@Hickmott2022_autoregulation]. Percentages would also require maximal testing, which is unwise alone as a novice (inference).
